Part 1: Submarine Design, Metallurgy & Stability

1. Metallurgy of Submarine Hulls: Why the Inner Hull Must Be Stronger

A submarine has a double-hull or partial double-hull construction:

  • Inner hull (pressure hull): Withstands external hydrostatic pressure at depth. Must resist elastic buckling and plastic collapse.
  • Outer hull (light hull): Provides hydrodynamic shape, protects internal systems, and houses ballast tanks. It is not pressure-tight and experiences minimal stress.

Why the inner hull is stronger:

At depth h h h, external pressure is:

P=ρgh P = \rho g h P=ρgh

where ρ≈1025 kg/m3 \rho \approx 1025 \, \text{kg/m}^3 ρ≈1025kg/m3 (seawater), g=9.81 m/s2 g = 9.81 \, \text{m/s}^2 g=9.81m/s2.

At 300 m depth:

P≈1025×9.81×300≈3.0 MPa (≈30 bar) P \approx 1025 \times 9.81 \times 300 \approx 3.0 \, \text{MPa} \, (\approx 30 \, \text{bar}) P≈1025×9.81×300≈3.0MPa(≈30bar)

This pressure acts uniformly on the inner hull, creating compressive hoop stress:

σθ=P⋅rt \sigma_{\theta} = \frac{P \cdot r}{t} σθ​=tP⋅r​

where r r r = hull radius, t t t = hull thickness.

If σθ \sigma_{\theta} σθ​ exceeds yield strength or causes buckling, catastrophic implosion occurs. Hence, the inner hull uses high-yield, low-alloy steels with excellent toughness at low temperatures.

Materials Used:

Hull Type Typical Materials Yield Strength (MPa) Key Properties
Inner (Pressure) Hull HY-80, HY-100, HY-130 (US); TI-6Al-4V (titanium, Russian Alfa-class); NS110 (modern) 550–900+ High yield, fracture toughness, weldability, corrosion resistance
Outer (Light) Hull Mild steel (A36), stainless cladding, composites 250–350 Formability, corrosion resistance, low cost

  • Inner hull steel (HY-100): High yield plateau, large plastic region before necking → absorbs energy without brittle fracture.

2. Ballast Tanks: Functions & Locations

Submarines use ballast tanks to control buoyancy and trim. Key types:

Tank Type Location Function
Main Ballast Tanks (MBTs) Between inner & outer hull, along sides & bottom Flood to submerge; blow with HP air to surface
Trim Tanks (Forward/Aft) Inside pressure hull, near bow/stern Fine-tune longitudinal balance (trim angle)
Negative Tank Usually forward, inside pressure hull Provides negative buoyancy for rapid dive; blown early in ascent
Safety Tank Often amidships Emergency buoyancy reserve
Compensation Tank Variable Adjusts for weight changes (e.g., torpedo firing)

Diagram: Ballast Tank Layout (Simplified) 

         [Outer Hull]
   ┌─────────────────────────┐
   │ MBT │ MBT │ MBT │ MBT   │ ← Main Ballast (floodable)
   │─────┴─────┴─────┴───────│
   │ [Pressure Hull Interior]│
   │ Neg │ Trim F │ Trim A   │ ← Negative + Trim Tanks
   └─────────────────────────┘
  • MBTs: Always vented at top; flood from bottom → air escapes, water enters → submarine loses buoyancy.
  • Trim/Negative: Pump-controlled; used for precise depth/angle control.

3. How a Submarine Surfaces & Submerges

Submerging:

  1. Open MBT vents → air escapes, seawater floods tanks.
  2. Buoyancy decreases → submarine becomes negatively buoyant.
  3. Use diving planes (bow/stern) to control descent angle.
  4. Trim tanks adjusted to maintain level dive.

Surfacing:

  1. Close MBT vents, inject high-pressure air → forces water out.
  2. Buoyancy increases → submarine rises.
  3. Blow negative tank early for positive lift.
  4. Trim tanks compensate for shifting center of gravity.
Submerging:          Surfacing:
  Air out              Air in (HP)
  Water in → ⬇         Water out → ⬆
  Negative buoyancy    Positive buoyancy

4. Role of Negative & Trim Tanks

  • Negative Tank: Provides instant negative buoyancy for emergency dives. During surfacing, it’s blown first to initiate ascent.
  • Trim Tanks: Maintain zero trim angle (level). When flooding MBTs, water distribution may shift G (center of gravity); trim tanks pump water fore/aft to realign G with B (center of buoyancy).

Without trim control, the submarine would pitch uncontrollably during depth changes.

5. Intact Stability: Transverse vs. Longitudinal (Surfaced vs. Submerged)

Surfaced Condition:

  • Behaves like a surface ship.
  • Transverse stability: Depends on waterplane area → large BMₜ (metacentric radius).
  • Longitudinal stability: Much larger BMₗ due to elongated waterplane.

Submerged Condition:

  • No waterplane → BM = 0 (no buoyancy shift with heel).
  • B (center of buoyancy) is fixed relative to hull.
  • Stability depends entirely on G-B separation:
    • G below B → stable (like a pendulum).
    • G above B → unstable.
Surfaced:          Submerged:
   M                   B
   |                   |
   B                   |
   |                   G (must be < B)
   G
  • Transverse GM (submerged): GMt=KB−KG GM_t = KB - KG GMt​=KB−KG (since BM = 0)
  • Longitudinal GM (submerged): Same formula, but G-B alignment is critical for pitch control.

6. Righting Moment: Mono-hull Ship vs. Submerged Submarine

Surface Ship:

  • Heel → B shifts outward → creates righting arm GZ.
  • M (metacenter) is above G → positive GM.
  • Righting Moment: RM=Δ⋅GZ=Δ⋅GM⋅sin⁡θ RM = \Delta \cdot GZ = \Delta \cdot GM \cdot \sin\theta RM=Δ⋅GZ=Δ⋅GM⋅sinθ

Submerged Submarine:

  • B does not shift (fully submerged, no waterplane).
  • No metacenter (M) → stability from G below B.
  • Righting Moment: RM=Δ⋅(KB−KG)⋅sin⁡θ RM = \Delta \cdot (KB - KG) \cdot \sin\theta RM=Δ⋅(KB−KG)⋅sinθ
Surface Ship:       Submarine (Submerged):
     M                    B
     |                    |
     B                    |
     |                    G
     G
   GZ = GM·sinθ         GZ = (KB-KG)·sinθ

Submarines have much smaller righting moments when submerged → rely on active control (planes, trim) rather than passive stability.

7. GM Longitudinal vs. Transverse in Submarines

Parameter Surfaced Submarine Submerged Submarine Surface Ship
GMₜ (Transverse) Large (waterplane exists) Small (KB – KG only) Large
GMₗ (Longitudinal) Very large (L² effect) Same as GMₜ (KB – KG) Very large
Stability Source Waterplane + G-B G-B only Waterplane + G-B
Risk Capsizing if GM too low Pitch/roll divergence if G > B Capsizing, parametric roll

Key Insight: In submerged condition, GMₗ ≈ GMₜ (both depend only on vertical G-B separation), unlike surface ships where GMₗ » GMₜ.

Part 2: Wave Mechanics for Ship Stability & Safety

1. Trochoidal Waves: Definition & Geometry

A trochoidal wave models real ocean waves more accurately than sinusoidal waves. It describes the path of a water particle as a trochoid curve—generated by a point on a rolling circle.

Definition:

A trochoid is the curve traced by a point at distance r r r from the center of a circle of radius R R R rolling along a straight line.

  • If r=R r = R r=R: Cycloid (sharp crest, flat trough)
  • If r<R r < R r<R: Prolate trochoid (realistic ocean wave)
  • If r>R r > R r>R: Curtate trochoid (not physical for waves)

Key Parameters:

  • R R R: Radius of rolling circle = L2π \frac{L}{2\pi} 2πL​, where L L L = wavelength
  • r r r: Radius of particle orbit = decreases with depth
  • Still Water Line (SWL): Datum at mean water level
  • Particle P: Moves in circular orbit; radius r r r at surface, decays exponentially with depth

Trochoidal Wave Diagram: 

        Crest
          *
         / \
        /   \      Particle P at crest:
       /     \     → Moving forward (→)
------*-------*---- Still Water Line (SWL)
     /         \
    /           \   Particle P at trough:
   /             \  → Moving backward (←)
  *               *
 Trough         Crest

Circle radius R = L/2π
Particle orbit radius r (≤ R)

Particle Motion:

  • At crest: P moves forward (in wave direction)
  • At trough: P moves backward
  • At SWL (rising): P moves upward
  • At SWL (falling): P moves downward

Orbit radius at depth z z z:

r(z)=r0⋅e−kz,k=2πL r(z) = r_0 \cdot e^{-kz}, \quad k = \frac{2\pi}{L} r(z)=r0​⋅e−kz,k=L2π​

2. Significant Wave Height (Hs H_s Hs​ or H1/3 H_{1/3} H1/3​)

Definition:

The average height of the highest one-third of waves in a record. It approximates what an experienced observer would report as “significant” wave height.

3. Natural Period of Roll (Tϕ T_\phi Tϕ​)

Derived from simple harmonic motion analogy:

Restoring moment for small heel ϕ \phi ϕ:

MR=Δ⋅GM⋅sin⁡ϕ≈Δ⋅GM⋅ϕ M_R = \Delta \cdot GM \cdot \sin\phi \approx \Delta \cdot GM \cdot \phi MR​=Δ⋅GM⋅sinϕ≈Δ⋅GM⋅ϕ

Moment of inertia about roll axis:

I=Δ⋅k2/g I = \Delta \cdot k^2 / g I=Δ⋅k2/g

where k k k = radius of gyration in roll \approx 0.35–0.45 \times B .

Equation of motion:

I⋅ϕ¨+Δ⋅GM⋅ϕ=0 I \cdot \ddot{\phi} + \Delta \cdot GM \cdot \phi = 0 I⋅ϕ¨​+Δ⋅GM⋅ϕ=0

Natural period:

Tϕ=2πIΔ⋅GM=2πk2g⋅GM T_\phi = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{I}{\Delta \cdot GM}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{k^2}{g \cdot GM}} Tϕ​=2πΔ⋅GMI​​=2πg⋅GMk2​​

Simplified empirical formula (Derrett’s):

T_\phi \approx \frac{C \cdot B}{\sqrt{GM}}, \quad C \approx 0.75–0.85

Tϕ≈0.8×32.60.885≈26.080.941≈27.7 s T_\phi \approx \frac{0.8 \times 32.6}{\sqrt{0.885}} \approx \frac{26.08}{0.941} \approx 27.7 \, \text{s} Tϕ​≈0.885​0.8×32.6​≈0.94126.08​≈27.7s

This is dangerously long → risk of synchronous rolling with typical ocean wave periods (8–15 s).

4. Synchronous Rolling & Parametric Rolling

Synchronous Rolling:

Occurs when wave encounter period TE T_E TE​ matches ship’s natural roll period Tϕ T_\phi Tϕ​.

Encounter period (for heading angle μ \mu μ):

TE=LwVw+Vscos⁡μ T_E = \frac{L_w}{V_w + V_s \cos\mu} TE​=Vw​+Vs​cosμLw​​

where Lw L_w Lw​ = wavelength, Vw V_w Vw​ = wave celerity, Vs V_s Vs​ = ship speed.

Danger: Even moderate waves can cause resonant roll amplification → capsizing (e.g., APL CHINA, 1988) .

APL CHINA Case:

  • Container ship in North Pacific storm
  • Large roll angles (>30°) → container losses
  • Cause: Synchronous rolling in beam seas + low GM
  • Solution: Increase GM (counterintuitive: usually mariners reduce GM for comfort) .

Parametric Rolling:

Occurs in head or following seas when wave passage modulates GM periodically.

Conditions:

  • Fine bow, wide stern (container ships, cruise vessels)
  • Wave length ≈ ship length
  • Ship speed such that pitch period ≈ ½ × roll period

Mechanism:

  • Crest amidships → waterplane narrows → GM decreases
  • Trough amidships → waterplane widens → GM increases
  • If GM variation frequency ≈ 2× roll frequency → parametric resonance → roll angles >40° possible.

Avoidance Strategies:

  1. Change speed → alter encounter period
  2. Alter course → move away from head/following seas
  3. Adjust GM (ballast transfer)
  4. Activate anti-roll tanks/fins

5. Virtual Gravity & Virtual Upright (Trochoidal Waves)

On a trochoidal wave, the effective gravity vector tilts due to centrifugal acceleration of water particles.

Virtual Gravity (g′ g' g′):

g′=g−ω2r g' = g - \omega^2 r g′=g−ω2r

where ω \omega ω = wave angular frequency, r r r = particle orbit radius.

Virtual Upright:

The direction perpendicular to the local wave slope (not horizontal). A ship on a wave crest “feels” upright relative to the sloped surface.

Danger to Small Craft:

  • Fishing vessels on steep waves → virtual upright misaligns with true vertical
  • Crew perceives stability when actually GZ is reduced
  • Sudden wave trough → loss of righting moment → capsize
True Vertical      Virtual Upright
     ↓                  ↖
     |                   \
     |                    \  Wave slope
-----*---------------------*---- SWL
     |                   /
     |                  /
     ↓                 ↙
  Gravity           Virtual Gravity

6. MSC Circular 1228: Avoiding Dangerous Situations

Core Assumptions:

  1. Waves are trochoidal, not sinusoidal.
  2. Ship motions are linear (small angles) — limitation in extreme seas.
  3. Resonant interactions dominate risk (synchronous roll, parametric roll, surf-riding).

Key Parameters:

Parameter Symbol Risk Threshold
Wave height Hw H_w Hw​ > 0.05 × LBP
Wave period Tw T_w Tw​ ≈ Tϕ T_\phi Tϕ​ or 0.5Tϕ 0.5 T_\phi 0.5Tϕ​
Encounter period TE T_E TE​ Match Tϕ T_\phi Tϕ​ → synchronous
GM — Too low → large rolls; too high → short, violent rolls

Limitations:

  • Assumes regular waves — real seas are irregular (spectral).
  • Does not account for wind drift, current, or loading changes.
  • Masters must observe actual Tw T_w Tw​, Hw H_w Hw​, and adjust speed/course proactively.

7. Surfing, Broaching, and Pooping

Surfing (Following Seas):

  • Ship speed ≈ wave celerity → vessel “surfs” down wave face.
  • Risk: Loss of steerage, broaching (sudden yaw to beam seas).

Broaching:

  • Stern lifted by wave → rudder/propeller emerge → loss of control.
  • Ship turns beam-to-sea → large roll moment → capsize.

Pooping (Stern Seas):

  • Wave breaks over stern → flooding, structural damage.

Avoidance:

  • Reduce speed in following seas > 0.7 × wave celerity.
  • Alter course to 30–45° off wave direction.

Subject: Avoiding Synchronous Rolling & Pooping in Adverse Weather

Observations Required:

Part 3: Tanker vs. Bulk Carrier Design & Safety

1. Inherent Strength: Tanker vs. Dry Cargo Ship

Tanker Advantages:

  • Continuous longitudinal strength: Cargo tanks act as integral part of hull girder → no large hatch openings.
  • Smaller hatchways: Only for inspection → minimal stress concentration.
  • Double bottom + double sides (post-MARPOL): Redundant protection, improved torsional rigidity.
  • Uniform cargo density: Liquid cargo distributes evenly → predictable shear/bending.

Bulk Carrier Disadvantages:

  • Large hatch openings (for grab/crane access) → reduce deck section modulus by 30–40%.
  • Stress concentrations at hatch corners → fatigue cracks.
  • Variable cargo density: Ore vs. grain → unpredictable loading, risk of hold flooding.
  • Single-skin construction (pre-2000s): Vulnerable to corrosion, grounding.
Tanker Hull:          Bulk Carrier Hull:
┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│  Small Hatches│      │  LARGE HATCHES   │ ← Weakens deck
├──────────────┤      ├──────────────────┤
│  Integral Tanks│      │  Topside/Hopper  │ ← Stress risers
└──────────────┘      └──────────────────┘

2. Freeboard Assignment: Why Tankers Get Less Freeboard

ILLC (International Load Line Convention) Objectives:

  1. Reserve buoyancy for wave immersion
  2. Limit deck edge immersion angle
  3. Ensure watertight integrity of openings
  4. Account for hull form (sheer, camber)
  5. Consider cargo type (permeability, shift risk)
  6. Structural strength (hull girder, hatch covers)
  7. Survivability after damage

Tanker vs. Bulk Carrier Freeboard:

Factor Tanker Bulk Carrier Effect on Freeboard
Hatch Size Small (inspection only) Very large (cargo access) Bulk carrier needs more freeboard to prevent wave ingress
Cargo Permeability ~95% (liquid) 60–90% (solid, air gaps) Tanker floods uniformly; bulk carrier risks free surface + shift
Hull Strength Continuous deck Hatch corners weaken deck Bulk carrier requires higher freeboard to reduce bending
Damage Stability Double hull compartments Single hold flooding → progressive Tanker survives 1-compartment damage better

Result: For same L, B, D → tanker assigned 0.5–1.5 m less freeboard than bulk carrier.

3. Pump Room Double Bottom: Survivability Enhancement

Regulatory Requirement (SOLAS II-1/12):

  • Cargo pumps in tankers must be in pump rooms with double bottom height ≥ 0.76 m (or equivalent protection).

Safety Benefits:

  1. Grounding protection: Double bottom absorbs impact → prevents cargo tank rupture.
  2. Flooding isolation: Pump room flooding ≠ cargo tank flooding → limits free surface effect.
  3. Fire safety: Pump room is gas-tight, separate from engine room → reduces explosion risk.
Tanker Midship Section:
┌─────────────────────┐
│  Cargo Tanks        │
├─────────────────────┤
│  Pump Room (Double Bottom)│ ← 0.76m+ protection
├─────────────────────┤
│  Engine Room        │
└─────────────────────┘

Without this, grounding could flood pump room + adjacent cargo tanks → loss of stability + fire hazard.

4. Corrosion in Tankers: Problems & Regulatory Solutions

Corrosion Mechanisms:

  • Cargo tank coating breakdown → seawater + oil residue → accelerated wastage.
  • Ballast tank corrosion: Poor coating, inadequate cathodic protection.
  • Stress corrosion cracking: High-tensile steel + residual stress + seawater.

Notable Losses:

  1. MV Sea Star (1997): ULCC, structural failure due to corroded deck plating → broke in two.
  2. MV Erika (1999): Single-hull tanker, corroded bottom plating → grounding → spill.
  3. MV Prestige (2002): Age + corrosion → hull fracture in storm.

Regulatory Solutions:

  • MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 13: Mandatory double hulls for tankers >5,000 DWT (phased out single hull by 2010).
  • IACS CSR (Common Structural Rules): Enhanced corrosion margins, coating standards.
  • ESP (Enhanced Survey Programme): Annual thickness measurements for tankers >10 years.

5. Bulk Carrier Design: Topside & Hopper Tanks

Why Included?

  1. Strength: Triangular structure → resists racking (transverse distortion).
  2. Stability: Lowers VCG (vertical center of gravity) → improves GM.
  3. Flooding control: Limits cargo shift + free surface in hold flooding.
  4. Ballast management: Dedicated tanks for trim/draft control.
Bulk Carrier Hold:
     Topside Tank
    /¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯\
   │              │
   │   CARGO      │
   │              │
    \____________/
     Hopper Tank

Safety Impact: After flooding of one hold, topside/hopper tanks prevent progressive flooding to adjacent holds → survivability.

6. Granular Sulphur Ban (Post-Arcadia, 1998)

Incident:

  • MV Arcadia: Bulk carrier, granular sulphur cargo → shifted like grain → angle of loll → capsized near Mumbai.

Why Banned?

  • Twindex behavior: Sulphur fines fluidize under vibration → acts like Bingham plastic (solid at rest, liquid when disturbed).
  • Angle of repose: ~35° → exceeds safe heel angle for many bulk carriers.
  • IMO MSC/Circ. 664: Prohibited carriage unless treated as grain (shifting boards, trimming).

Lesson: Cargo classification must account for dynamic behavior, not just static density.

7. Single-Skin Bulk Carrier Sinking Scenario

Typical Failure Sequence:

  1. Hatch cover failure (corrosion + overpressure) → seawater ingress.
  2. Hold flooding → free surface effect → GM reduces.
  3. Bulkhead collapse (designed for cargo, not water pressure) → progressive flooding.
  4. Loss of longitudinal strength → hull girder fails → rapid sinking.
Progressive Flooding:
Hold 1 → Bulkhead → Hold 2 → Bulkhead → Hold 3
  ↓        ↓         ↓        ↓         ↓
Flooded  Failed    Flooded  Failed    Flooded → Sinking

Survivability Issue: Single-skin bulk carriers cannot survive two adjacent holds flooded.

8. IMO/IACS Formal Safety Assessment (1995–2000)

Main Failures Identified:

  1. Design: Hatch covers under-designed for wave loads.
  2. Construction: Poor welding, corrosion allowances insufficient.
  3. Operation: Overloading, improper ballasting, delayed maintenance.
  4. Survey: Inadequate thickness measurements.

Solutions:

Regulatory (IMO) Industry (IACS)
SOLAS XII: Strengthened hatch covers, double sides for new bulk carriers >150m CSR Bulk Carriers: Enhanced scantlings, fatigue analysis
ISM Code: Mandatory safety management ESP: Annual surveys for bulk carriers >10 years
Load Line Amendments: Bow height, hatch coaming height UR Z10: Corrosion margin increases

Result: Bulk carrier losses dropped >70% post-2005.

Part 5: ROPAX Stability & SOLAS 90/90+50 Standards

1. Case Studies: Al Salaam & Boccaccio 98

MV Al Salaam (2006, Red Sea)

  • Loss: 950+ lives
  • Cause: Fire in vehicle deck → water accumulation from firefighting → free surface effect → capsized.
  • Stability Failure:
    • Firefighting water not pumped out → GM reduced to negative.
    • Passengers ran to one side → heeling moment exceeded righting moment.
    • No damage stability compliance (pre-SOLAS 90).

MV Boccaccio 98 (1992, Baltic Sea)

  • Loss: 140+ lives
  • Cause: Bow door failure → seawater ingress on vehicle deck → free surface + free communication → capsized in 30 min.
  • Stability Failure:
    • Large undivided vehicle deck → water spread across beam.
    • Insufficient reserve buoyancy → rapid downflooding.

Common Factor: Both lacked SOLAS 90 damage stability → could not survive one-compartment flooding.

2. SOLAS 90 Standard for ROPAX Ships

Definition:

SOLAS 90 (1990 amendments) requires ROPAX ships to survive flooding of any one compartment with:

  • Residual GM ≥ 0.05 m
  • Righting lever GZ ≥ 0.1 m over 30° range
  • Equilibrium heel ≤ 15°

Key Requirements:

  1. Subdivision: Vehicle decks divided by watertight bulkheads.
  2. Damage stability calculations: Probabilistic method (not deterministic).
  3. Free surface correction: Account for water accumulation on car decks.

Impact: Pre-1990 ROPAX ships failed this standard → required retrofits or phase-out.

3. SOLAS 90+50 (Stockholm Agreement, 1996)

Background:

After Estonia disaster (1994), IMO adopted Stockholm Agreement (1996), enhancing SOLAS 90.

Key Provisions:

  • Additional 50 cm freeboard (hence “+50”) for ROPAX ships.
  • Higher damage stability: Survive flooding with 50 cm water on vehicle deck.
  • Mandatory bow door locks + CCTV monitoring.
  • Phased compliance: Existing ships to comply by 2010.

A and Amax Parameters:

  • A: Actual subdivision index (probability of surviving damage).
  • Amax: Minimum required index (function of ship length, N passengers).

Compliance Rule:

A≥Amax=1−1000Ls+N+1500 A \geq A_{max} = 1 - \frac{1000}{L_s + N + 1500} A≥Amax​=1−Ls​+N+15001000​

Where Ls L_s Ls​ = subdivision length, N N N = passenger capacity.

Q.1 Purpose of Common Structural Rules (CSR) and IACS Approaches

A. Purpose of Introducing CSR

The Common Structural Rules (CSR) were introduced by the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) to address the following key objectives:

  1. Harmonization of Structural Standards:

    • Eliminate differences in structural rules among classification societies (e.g., ABS, DNV, LR, NKK).
    • Ensure consistent safety levels across the global fleet.

  2. Improved Safety:

    • Reduce structural failures (e.g., bulk carrier sinkings, tanker breakups) by adopting uniform, science-based standards.
    • Address lessons learned from incidents like MV Derbyshire (1980), Erika (1999), and Prestige (2002).

  3. Efficiency in Design and Construction:

    • Streamline approval processes for shipyards and owners.
    • Reduce duplicative work (e.g., multiple society approvals for the same design).

  4. Compliance with IMO’s Goal-Based Standards (GBS):

    • Align with IMO’s GBS framework (Tier I–IV) to ensure performance-based rather than purely prescriptive rules.

  5. Innovation and Flexibility:

    • Allow for new materials, designs, and technologies while maintaining safety.

B. Fundamental Approaches of IACS in Developing CSR-OT + BC

The CSR for Oil Tankers (CSR-OT) and Bulk Carriers (CSR-BC) were developed using the following fundamental approaches:

Approach Description Application in CSR
Risk-Based Design Uses probabilistic methods to assess structural reliability. Load cases (e.g., hogging, sagging, torsion) are analyzed for probability of failure.
Performance-Based Standards Focuses on what the structure must achieve (e.g., strength, fatigue life) rather than how to achieve it. Functional requirements (e.g., “The ship must survive a grounding event without catastrophic failure”).
Harmonized Scantling Calculations Unified formulas for plate thickness, stiffeners, and girder dimensions. Common equations for longitudinal strength, buckling, and fatigue.
First-Principles Analysis Uses fundamental engineering principles (e.g., finite element analysis) to derive requirements. Direct strength analysis for hull girder, local strength, and fatigue.
Safety Margins Incorporates safety factors to account for uncertainties (e.g., material properties, loading conditions). Partial safety factors for yield strength, corrosion, and dynamic loads.
Validation Through Testing Uses full-scale measurements, model tests, and FE analysis to validate rules. IACS Joint Industry Projects (e.g., Tanker Structural Cooperative Forum, Bulk Carrier Safety Assessment).

Q.2 Class Notations for Bulk Carriers (ECR) vs. SOLAS Ch. XIII

A. Class Notations for Bulk Carriers (ECR - Enhanced Common Rules)

The Enhanced Common Rules (ECR) for bulk carriers introduce class notations based on cargo density and structural strength requirements. The primary notations are:

Notation Description Cargo Density Range Structural Strength
BC-A High-strength bulk carrier > 1.75 t/m³ (e.g., iron ore, coal) Designed for high-density cargoes with increased scantlings.
BC-B Standard bulk carrier 1.0–1.75 t/m³ (e.g., grain, bauxite) Moderate scantlings for typical bulk cargoes.
BC-C Lightweight bulk carrier < 1.0 t/m³ (e.g., light grain, wood chips) Reduced scantlings (lighter cargoes require less structural strength).

B. Comparison with SOLAS Ch. XIII Hull Strength Requirements

Aspect ECR (Class Notations) SOLAS Ch. XIII
Basis Performance-based (cargo density, loading conditions). Prescriptive (minimum scantlings, general requirements).
Cargo Density Consideration Explicitly accounts for cargo density (BC-A, BC-B, BC-C). No direct classification by density (general requirements for all bulk carriers).
Structural Strength Tailored scantlings based on cargo type. Uniform minimum requirements (e.g., plate thickness, stiffener spacing).
Hull Girder Strength Detailed calculations for hogging, sagging, and torsion. Simplified formulas (e.g., longitudinal strength formula).
Fatigue Assessment Mandatory fatigue analysis for high-stress areas. No explicit fatigue requirements (left to class societies).
Corrosion Allowance Differentiated corrosion margins (e.g., 3 mm for BC-A, 2 mm for BC-C). General corrosion allowance (e.g., 2 mm for ballast tanks).

C. Why Cargo Density Matters in Strength Requirements

The density of cargo directly influences the structural loads on a bulk carrier in the following ways:

  1. Hull Girder Bending Moments:

    • Higher-density cargoes (e.g., iron ore at ~2.5 t/m³) create greater bending moments on the hull girder.
    • Example: A BC-A ship (carrying iron ore) experiences ~50% higher bending moments than a BC-C ship (carrying light grain).

  2. Local Strength (Plate and Stiffeners):

    • High-density cargoes require thicker plates and stronger stiffeners to prevent buckling and yielding.
    • Example: BC-A ships have 20–30% thicker bottom plates than BC-C ships.

  3. Shear Forces:

    • Dense cargoes increase transverse shear forces on the hull, requiring stronger web frames and transverse bulkheads.

  4. Dynamic Loads:

    • Heavy cargoes (e.g., iron ore) can cause impact loads during loading/unloading, requiring reinforced hopper tanks and side shells.

  5. Stability and Trim:

    • Dense cargoes lower the center of gravity (KG), improving stability but increasing hull stresses.
    • Light cargoes (e.g., grain) raise KG, reducing stability but reducing hull stresses.

  6. Corrosion and Wear:

    • Abrasive cargoes (e.g., iron ore, coal) accelerate wear and corrosion in cargo holds, requiring additional corrosion margins.

Q.4 Prescriptive Standards vs. Goal-Based Standards (GBS)

A. Why Existing Construction Standards Are Called Prescriptive

Prescriptive standards are rules that explicitly specify how to achieve compliance by providing detailed, step-by-step requirements for design, materials, and construction. They are rigid and do not allow for alternative solutions, even if they achieve the same safety level.

Characteristics of Prescriptive Standards

  1. Detailed Requirements:
    • Specify exact dimensions, materials, and methods (e.g., “The minimum plate thickness in cargo holds must be 15 mm.”).
  2. No Flexibility:
    • No room for innovation or alternative designs that might achieve the same safety level.
  3. Based on Past Experience:
    • Developed from historical data and incidents (e.g., SOLAS rules after Titanic).
  4. Uniform Application:
    • Same rules apply to all ships of a given type, regardless of specific risks.

Examples of Prescriptive Standards

Standard Prescriptive Requirement Source
SOLAS II-1 “The minimum freeboard for a bulk carrier must be calculated using the ILLC 1966 formulas.” IMO
ILLC 1966 “The minimum plate thickness for a ship’s bottom shell must be t = 0.02L + 5 mm, where L is the ship’s length.” IMO
Class Society Rules (Pre-CSR) “The spacing between transverse frames in cargo holds must not exceed 2.5 m.” ABS, DNV, LR
MARPOL Annex I (Pre-2010) “Oil tankers must have a double bottom with a height of at least B/15 or 2 m, whichever is less.” IMO

B. Merits of GBS Over Prescriptive Standards

Aspect Prescriptive Standards Goal-Based Standards (GBS)
Flexibility Rigid (no alternatives allowed). Flexible (allows innovative designs that meet functional requirements).
Innovation Discourages innovation (must follow exact rules). Encourages innovation (new materials, designs, and technologies can be used if they meet goals).
Safety Focus Compliance-based (follow the rules = safe). Performance-based (meet the safety goals = safe, regardless of method).
Adaptability Difficult to update (requires rule changes for new technologies). Easily adaptable (functional requirements can be met with new solutions).
Risk Assessment One-size-fits-all (same rules for all ships). Risk-based (rules tailored to specific risks and loading conditions).
Global Harmonization Differences between class societies (e.g., ABS vs. DNV rules). Harmonized (IACS CSR aligns with IMO GBS).
Cost Efficiency May lead to over-design (rules may require more material than necessary). Optimized design (only what is needed to meet goals).

C. Lack of Innovation Due to Prescriptive Standards: Case Studies

(a) Typical Bulk Carrier (BC) Sinking Scenario

Incident: MV Derbyshire (1980) – Largest British ship lost at sea (180,000 DWT bulk carrier).

  • Prescriptive Rules Followed:
    • Met ILLC 1966 freeboard requirements.
    • Complied with class society rules for plate thickness and stiffener spacing.
  • Structural Failures:
    1. Hull Girder Failure:
      • Hogging stress from uneven cargo distribution (heavy iron ore in center holds, light ballast in ends).
      • Prescriptive rules did not account for dynamic loads (e.g., sloshing in ballast tanks).
    2. Buckling of Bottom Plates:
      • Thin plates (15–18 mm) buckled under high compressive stresses.
      • No fatigue analysis was required under prescriptive rules.
    3. Poor Watertight Integrity:
      • Hatch covers were not watertight (prescriptive rules allowed this).
      • Flooding through hatch covers led to loss of stability.
  • Why Prescriptive Rules Failed:
    • No consideration of loading conditions (e.g., alternate hold loading).
    • No fatigue life assessment (ship was 10 years old but had severe corrosion).
    • No redundancy in structural design (single-skin hull).

Lesson: Prescriptive rules did not account for real-world loading and fatigue, leading to catastrophic failure.

(b) Double Hull (DH) Tankers

Incidents: Erika (1999), Prestige (2002) – Single-hull tankers that broke in half, causing massive oil spills.

  • Prescriptive Rules Followed:
    • Met MARPOL Annex I (pre-2010) requirements for single-hull tankers.
    • Complied with class society rules for plate thickness and corrosion margins.
  • Structural Failures:
    1. Corrosion in Cargo Tanks:
      • No mandatory coating standards (PSPC was introduced later).
      • Thickness reduced to 1–2 mm in some areas (original: 12–15 mm).
    2. Brittle Fracture:
      • Low-temperature corrosion (cold seawater + sulfur in crude oil) → embrittlement of steel.
      • No fracture toughness requirements in prescriptive rules.
    3. Poor Structural Redundancy:
      • Single hull → no secondary barrier in case of grounding.
      • No double bottom → direct contact with seawater accelerated corrosion.
  • Why Prescriptive Rules Failed:
    • No corrosion monitoring (only visual inspections were required).
    • No fatigue analysis (tankers were 20+ years old with no fatigue life assessment).
    • No requirement for double hulls until MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 13G (2010).

Lesson: Prescriptive rules did not prevent corrosion or brittle fracture, leading to structural failures.

④ Useful Coating Life as per PSPC

  • Definition: The minimum expected lifespan of a coating system before major maintenance or recoating is required.
  • PSPC Requirement (IMO MSC.215(82)):
    • 15 years for ballast tanks (most critical area).
    • 10 years for cargo tanks (oil tankers).

    1. Coating Type:
      • Epoxy coatings (15+ years).
      • Zinc-rich coatings (10–15 years).
    2. Surface Preparation:
      • Sa 2.5 blast cleaning (near-white metal) → longer life.
      • Poor preparation → premature failure.
    3. Environmental Conditions:
      • Ballast tanks (seawater, high humidity) → shorter life.
      • Cargo tanks (oil, chemicals) → longer life.
    4. Application Quality:
      • Proper curing → better adhesion.
      • Incorrect application → peeling, cracking.
    5. Maintenance:
      • Regular inspections → extend life.
      • No maintenance → reduce life to 5–7 years.
  • Verification:
    • IACS UR Z10.4 requires annual inspections to confirm coating performance.
    • Ultrasonic Thickness Measurements (UTM) to monitor corrosion.

⑤ Net Scantling (GBS)

  • Definition: The minimum required dimensions (e.g., plate thickness, stiffener size) of a ship’s structural members after accounting for corrosion, wear, and fatigue.
  • Purpose:
    • Ensure structural integrity throughout the ship’s design life (typically 25 years for bulk carriers and tankers).
    • Provide a safety margin against yielding, buckling, and fatigue failure.
  • Calculation: 
    Net Scantling = Gross Scantling – Corrosion Allowance – Wear Allowance
    • Gross Scantling: Nominal thickness (e.g., 20 mm plate).
    • Corrosion Allowance: Extra thickness to account for corrosion (e.g., 2–3 mm for ballast tanks).
    • Wear Allowance: Extra thickness for abrasive cargoes (e.g., 1–2 mm for iron ore carriers).
  • GBS Requirement (Tier III):
    • Net scantlings must meet functional requirements (e.g., strength, fatigue life).
    • Verification through direct calculation or finite element analysis (FEA).
  • Example (Bulk Carrier):
    • Gross Plate Thickness: 20 mm.
    • Corrosion Allowance: 3 mm.
    • Wear Allowance: 1 mm (for iron ore).
    • Net Scantling: 20 – 3 – 1 = 16 mm (minimum required after 25 years).

IMO Fire Safety Regulations: Layers of Protection & SOLAS Chapter II-2

1. Layers of Protection in Fire Safety (IMO Approach)

The IMO’s fire safety philosophy is based on four layers of protection, designed to address fire at every stage:

Layer Objective Key Measures (SOLAS Ch. II-2)
Prevention Minimize the probability of fire ignition. - Restrictions on ignition sources (e.g., electrical equipment, hot work permits).- Use of non-combustible materials in construction.- Smoking restrictions in cargo holds and accommodation spaces.
Fire Spread Prevention Limit the spread of fire if ignition occurs. - Structural fire divisions (A, B, C class bulkheads/decks).- Fire doors (self-closing, fire-rated).- Fire dampers in ventilation systems.- Thermal insulation to delay heat transfer.
Fire Extinction Detect and extinguish fires effectively. - Fixed fire extinguishing systems (CO₂, foam, water mist).- Portable extinguishers (dry chemical, foam, CO₂).- Fire main system (hose reels, hydrants).- Automatic sprinklers in accommodation spaces.
Safety of Life Ensure safe evacuation and survival of crew and passengers. - Emergency escape routes (protected, illuminated).- Firefighter’s outfits and breathing apparatus.- Lifesaving appliances (lifeboats, liferafts).- Fire drills and training.

2. Fire Safety Objectives, Functional Requirements & SOLAS Ch. II-2

A. Fire Safety Objectives (IMO)

The primary objectives of IMO’s fire safety regulations are:

  1. Prevent fire occurrence (minimize ignition sources).
  2. Limit fire growth (contain fire to the compartment of origin).
  3. Ensure structural integrity (prevent collapse due to fire).
  4. Facilitate evacuation (safe escape routes).
  5. Enable fire suppression (effective extinguishing systems).
  6. Protect adjacent spaces (prevent fire spread).

B. Functional Requirements (SOLAS Ch. II-2)

SOLAS Chapter II-2 (Fire Protection, Fire Detection, and Fire Extinction) is performance-based, meaning it specifies what must be achieved rather than how to achieve it. The functional requirements include:

Functional Requirement Purpose Example Regulations in SOLAS Ch. II-2
Containment of Fire Fire must be contained within the compartment of origin for a specified time. - A-60, B-15, C-0 class divisions (Reg. 9).- Fire doors (Reg. 9.4).- Fire dampers (Reg. 9.7).
Limitation of Fire Spread Prevent fire from spreading to adjacent compartments. - Structural fire integrity (Reg. 9).- Thermal insulation (Reg. 9.2).- Non-combustible materials (Reg. 3).
Extinction of Fire Provide means to detect and extinguish fires. - Fixed fire extinguishing systems (Reg. 10).- Portable extinguishers (Reg. 10.2).- Fire main system (Reg. 10.1).
Protection of Escape Routes Ensure safe evacuation in case of fire. - Protected escape routes (Reg. 13).- Emergency lighting (Reg. 13.3).- Low-location lighting (Reg. 13.3.2).
Structural Integrity Maintain ship’s structural strength during and after a fire. - Fire resistance ratings (A-60, B-15, etc.).- Load-bearing capacity (Reg. 9.2.2).

3. Specialty of SOLAS Chapter II-2 Arrangement

SOLAS Chapter II-2 is unique because it:

  1. Adopts a Performance-Based Approach:
    • Specifies objectives and functional requirements rather than prescriptive solutions.
    • Allows innovative designs (e.g., alternative fire suppression systems) if they meet the same safety level.
  2. Incorporates Risk-Based Design:
    • Fire Risk Assessment (FRA) can be used to justify alternative arrangements (Reg. 17).
    • Encourages design improvements (e.g., safe return to port concept).
  3. Covers All Ship Types:
    • Applies to passenger ships, cargo ships, and tankers with specific amendments for each.
  4. Regularly Updated:
    • Amendments incorporate lessons from incidents (e.g., Scandinavian Star, Emma Maersk).

4. Structural Fire Divisions on a Ship

A. Types of Fire Divisions (SOLAS Reg. 9)

Structural fire divisions are classified based on their fire resistance and ability to prevent fire spread. The three main classes are:

Class Fire Resistance Rating Purpose Typical Applications
A-0 0 minutes No fire resistance (used for non-critical spaces). Store rooms, non-essential spaces.
A-15 15 minutes Low fire resistance (delays fire spread). Corridors, stairways (in some cases).
A-30 30 minutes Moderate fire resistance. Accommodation bulkheads, some cargo holds.
A-60 60 minutes High fire resistance (prevents fire spread for 60 mins). Primary fire divisions (e.g., between cargo holds and accommodation).
B-0 0 minutes Non-combustible materials but no insulation. External bulkheads (non-load-bearing).
B-15 15 minutes Non-combustible + insulation (delays temperature rise). Some machinery spaces.
C Non-combustible No fire resistance rating but non-combustible (e.g., steel). Decks in open areas, non-fire-risk spaces.

B. Purpose of Structural Fire Divisions

  1. Contain Fire: Prevent fire from spreading beyond the compartment of origin.
  2. Delay Fire Spread: Provide time for evacuation and firefighting.
  3. Protect Critical Spaces: Shield accommodation, control stations, and escape routes.
  4. Maintain Structural Integrity: Ensure the ship does not collapse during a fire.

5. Fire Bulkheads and Decks: Testing Methods

A. Standard Fire Test (SOLAS Reg. 3.2)

The standard fire test evaluates the fire resistance of bulkheads and decks. It involves:

  1. Exposure to a Standard Fire Curve:
    • A time-temperature curve simulating a fully developed fire.
    • Temperature rises according to the formula: T = 345 log₁₀(8t + 1), where t = time in minutes.
  2. Criteria for Passing:
    • Integrity: No flames or hot gases pass through.
    • Insulation: Temperature rise on the unexposed side does not exceed:
      • 140°C above ambient (average).
      • 180°C above ambient (at any point).
    • Load-bearing capacity: Must withstand mechanical stress during the test.

B. Non-Combustibility Test (SOLAS Reg. 3.1)

  • Purpose: Ensure materials do not contribute to fire spread.
  • Test Method (ISO 1182):
    • A small sample is exposed to 750°C for 5 minutes in a furnace.
    • Passing Criteria:
      • No flame propagation.
      • Temperature rise ≤ 30°C in the furnace.
      • Weight loss ≤ 50% of the original sample.

7. Case Study: Scandinavian Star (1990)

A. Incident Overview

  • Date: April 7, 1990.
  • Ship: Scandinavian Star (passenger/vehicle ferry).
  • Casualties: 159 deaths (one of the deadliest maritime disasters in peacetime).
  • Cause: Fire originated in a car deck, spread rapidly due to:
    • Inadequate fire divisions (B-class bulkheads instead of A-class).
    • Poor fire detection (no sprinklers in car decks).
    • Delayed evacuation (smoke spread to accommodation via ventilation systems).
    • Failure of fire doors (not self-closing).

B. Lessons Learned & SOLAS Amendments

  1. Stricter Fire Division Requirements:
    • Car decks now require A-60 class divisions (previously B-0 or B-15).
  2. Improved Fire Detection:
    • Automatic sprinklers mandatory in car decks and special category spaces (Reg. 10.2.1.3).
  3. Enhanced Ventilation Control:
    • Fire dampers must automatically close in case of fire (Reg. 9.7).
  4. Better Escape Routes:
    • Protected stairways and low-location lighting (Reg. 13).
  5. Human Element:
    • Mandatory fire drills and crew training (SOLAS Ch. II-2/15).

8. Significance of Insulation and Cable Penetrations in Fire Bulkheads/Decks

A. Insulation

  • Purpose:
    • Delays heat transfer to the unexposed side of the bulkhead/deck.
    • Prevents fire spread by maintaining temperature rise limits (140°C avg, 180°C max).
  • Materials:
    • Mineral wool, ceramic fiber, or calcium silicate (non-combustible).
  • Case Study: Emma Maersk (2006)
    • Issue: Fire in engine room spread via unprotected cable penetrations.
    • Lesson: Cable penetrations must be sealed with fire-resistant materials (e.g., fire-stopping systems).
    • SOLAS Requirement: Reg. 9.2.3 mandates fire-resistant sealing for all penetrations.

B. Cable Penetrations

  • Risk: Fire can spread through gaps where cables pass through bulkheads/decks.
  • Solution:
    • Fire-stopping systems (e.g., intumescent seals, fire-resistant putty).
    • Tested to the same fire resistance as the bulkhead (e.g., A-60 penetration = A-60 seal).
  • Emma Maersk Incident (2006):
    • Fire spread from the engine room to accommodation via unprotected cable penetrations.
    • Result: SOLAS amendments now require strict testing of cable transits (Reg. 9.2.3.2).

IMO’s passenger-ship safety initiative is built on the idea that prevention comes first, but if a casualty occurs, the ship should remain survivable—ideally acting as its own “best lifeboat” while returning safely to port or supporting an orderly abandonment. The initiative became necessary because very large cruise ships can carry several thousand people, have complex “hotel” spaces and fire loads, and can overwhelm normal evacuation and search-and-rescue arrangements even when formally compliant with older SOLAS and Load Line provisions. imo

Five pillars

Pillar Meaning Practical example
1. Prevention Reduce the probability of fire, collision, grounding, flooding, and operational error before they become casualties Improved fire prevention in atria and accommodation, improved escape arrangements, bridge/navigation safety, contingency planning, and passenger-ship-specific STCW training in crowd management and crisis management. imo
2. Improved survivability Design the ship so that, after defined damage, people can remain safe on board and the ship can proceed under its own power to a port of refuge Redundant propulsion, steering, electrical distribution, fire main, communications, detection, bilge/ballast and watertight-door systems; safe areas; emergency management from a safety centre. imo
3. Regulatory flexibility Permit innovative technologies and arrangements without reducing the required safety outcome SOLAS alternative design and arrangements provisions permit a designer to demonstrate, through rigorous assessment, that a novel fire-safety or evacuation arrangement achieves at least an equivalent level of safety. imo
4. Operation remote from SAR facilities Recognize that rapid outside rescue may be impossible in polar, oceanic, remote-island, or poorly served areas Voyage planning, external-support arrangements with SAR authorities, recovery techniques, and procedures for rescuing people from survival craft or the water. imo
5. Health, safety and medical care Maintain passenger survival and wellbeing during an extended onboard emergency or evacuation Medical-safety programmes, safe-area medical capacity, sanitation, water, food, ventilation, temperature control and cold-water survival guidance. imo

A useful exam conclusion is: the five pillars move safety from a narrow “abandon ship quickly” philosophy toward “prevent, contain, survive, return safely, and evacuate only when necessary.”

Why new standards were needed

Large cruise ships were already expected to comply with applicable SOLAS and ILLC requirements. IMO’s concern was whether regulations, many drafted before the newest very large passenger ships existed, fully addressed the operational reality of an emergency on such ships. imo

Scale of persons on board

A large cruise ship may have thousands of passengers plus crew. The consequences of a single major fire, blackout, collision, grounding, or flooding event can therefore be disproportionate.

Evacuating such a population is difficult because many passengers:

  • Are unfamiliar with ship layout, alarm signals, muster procedures and lifeboat embarkation.
  • May be elderly, disabled, injured, accompanied by children, or unable to communicate in the working language of the crew.
  • May panic, move against crew instructions, become separated from families, or congest stairways and embarkation areas.

The key question was not simply whether the ship carried enough lifeboat seats. It was whether people could reach, board, launch, survive in, and be recovered from survival craft in severe weather.

Fire vulnerability

Cruise ships contain high fire loads and complex hotel-type spaces:

  • Cabins, restaurants, galleys, laundries, theatres, retail areas and entertainment spaces.
  • Long accommodation corridors and multi-deck vertical spaces such as atria.
  • Extensive HVAC systems that can spread smoke if not correctly isolated.
  • Electrical and machinery systems whose loss may impair detection, communication, propulsion, lighting, pumps and evacuation.

IMO specifically recognized fire as a particular vulnerability of large cruise ships because hotel services create inherent ignition and fire-spread risks. imo

Survivability rather than immediate abandonment

Traditional regulations were strongly oriented to lifesaving appliances and evacuation. The large-passenger-ship initiative recognized that, in difficult weather or remote waters, abandoning a large ship may be more dangerous than remaining aboard a damaged but stable, powered and habitable vessel.

Thus, for casualties below a defined threshold, the design target is:

Casualty occurs
      ↓
Detect and contain it
      ↓
Keep propulsion, steering, power and communications available
      ↓
Move passengers into protected safe areas
      ↓
Return safely to port under own propulsion

If the casualty exceeds the threshold, the ship must still remain viable long enough for controlled evacuation and abandonment. IMO defined the “time for orderly evacuation and abandonment” as the time from the casualty threshold being exceeded until all persons have abandoned safely; the design work considered a viability period of at least three hours. imo

Training requirements

Existing STCW requirements

Under STCW Regulation V/2 and Code section A‑V/2, training is assigned according to a person’s duties.

Personnel Required competence
Crew or other personnel listed to assist passengers during an emergency Crowd management training
Masters, chief mates, chief engineers, second engineers and persons responsible for passenger safety in emergency situations Approved crisis management and human behaviour training
Personnel with safety duties Familiarization with emergency procedures, use of lifesaving appliances, emergency communications, passenger assistance and shipboard muster roles
All seafarers Basic safety training, including firefighting, personal survival, first aid and personal safety/social responsibility, as applicable

Crowd-management competence covers controlling passengers during emergencies, locating and assisting people needing help, communicating clearly, managing passenger movement and avoiding panic. Crisis-management and human-behaviour competence includes organizing emergency procedures, using available resources, maintaining communications and controlling the human response to an emergency. wwwcdn.imo

Why this may still be inadequate

The weakness is often not the existence of certificates, but the gap between classroom competence and a complex real casualty involving multiple failures, smoke, darkness, language barriers, injury, loss of communications and rapidly changing stability.

A serious casualty can combine:

Fire or flooding
+ loss of electrical power
+ smoke / impaired visibility
+ disabled lifts and communications
+ frightened passengers
+ partial loss of propulsion or steering
+ difficult weather
= a systems-and-human-factors emergency

Training can be inadequate where drills are too predictable, announced in advance, conducted in benign weather, or restricted to individual departments rather than testing bridge–engine–hotel–security–medical coordination.

Examples of shortcomings

Herald of Free Enterprise (1987). The ferry sailed with bow doors open. The immediate technical condition was simple—water entered the vehicle deck—but the underlying failures included weak operational controls, unclear responsibility, inadequate verification of door closure, and poor safety management. Water on the undivided vehicle deck rapidly caused a severe free-surface effect and capsize. This illustrates why bridge teams, vehicle-deck personnel and senior officers need robust closed-loop reporting and challenge-response procedures, not merely familiarity with a checklist.

Scandinavian Star (1990). The fire demonstrated the importance of competent firefighting command, smoke control, communications, emergency lighting, passenger guidance and crew familiarity with the vessel. A passenger vessel’s crew must be able to keep escape routes tenable and direct people away from smoke, not merely fight the fire.

Estonia (1994). The loss highlighted the fatal consequences of rapid ingress onto a ro-ro deck. The event requires effective damage recognition, watertight-integrity management, immediate reduction of speed or course alteration where appropriate, passenger control and timely—but orderly—evacuation decisions.

Additional training proposed

A credible enhanced programme should include the following:

  • Integrated casualty drills: bridge, engine room, safety centre, firefighting teams, hotel department, medical team, security and evacuation teams exercise together.
  • Scenario-based fire drills: fire in an atrium, galley, cabin corridor, laundry, vehicle deck or machinery space; include smoke migration, ventilation shutdown and a blocked escape route.
  • Flooding and damage-control drills: simulated progressive flooding, watertight-door management, bilge/pump limitations, stability assessment and safe-area relocation.
  • Blackout drills: loss of main power, degraded communications, emergency generator operation, emergency steering, emergency lighting and manual procedures.
  • Safe-return-to-port drills: maintain propulsion, steering, navigation, accommodation support, food, sanitation, medical care and communications while a main vertical zone is unavailable.
  • Crowd dynamics: family separation, mobility-impaired passengers, multiple languages, aggressive behaviour, passenger refusal to comply and misinformation management.
  • Command decision exercises: tabletop and simulator practice for the master and emergency-management team to decide between containment/return to port and abandonment.
  • Realistic evacuation drills: include darkness, restricted routes, simulated injured persons and timed muster/embarkation—but without creating unsafe drill conditions.
  • Shore-side integration: company emergency response, port authorities, flag State, coastal State, SAR services, hospitals and salvage support.

Estonia, 1994 Failure of bow-visors/ramps and subsequent vehicle-deck flooding can cause extremely rapid loss of stability Strengthened ro-ro passenger-ship stability measures, bow-door/locking and monitoring requirements, and regional residual-stability measures such as the Stockholm Agreement framework.

The common lesson is that passenger safety cannot be treated only as hull strength or only as lifeboat capacity. It is a combined problem of design, watertight integrity, fire safety, human behaviour, training, command, maintenance and shore support.

Safe Return to Port

Why amendments appear in SOLAS II-1 and II-2

They are split because safe return to port must address both flooding survivability and fire survivability.

SOLAS chapter Main casualty concern Role in Safe Return to Port
Chapter II-1 Subdivision, stability, machinery and electrical installations; especially flooding Requires the ship to retain required capability after a flooding casualty within the defined damage threshold, including assessment of flooding, compartment integrity and essential systems.
Chapter II-2 Fire protection, detection, containment and extinction Requires the vessel to retain essential systems outside the fire-affected main vertical zone, provide safe areas and support orderly evacuation/abandonment if the fire casualty exceeds the threshold. imo

A collision may flood machinery spaces, electrical rooms or compartments and threaten stability; a fire may disable an entire main vertical zone, fill escape routes with smoke, or sever cables and pipework. Therefore, a single chapter could not adequately regulate both failure modes.

Accident categories

For this subject, accident categories may be expressed as:

  • Flooding casualty: collision, grounding, hull breach, pipe rupture, shell-door failure, progressive compartment flooding.
  • Fire or explosion casualty: machinery-space fire, cabin fire, galley fire, electrical fire, vehicle-deck fire, fire in an atrium or service space.
  • Loss of essential-function casualty: blackout, propulsion failure, steering failure, loss of navigation, loss of firefighting water, loss of communications.
  • Evacuation/SAR casualty: a situation in which the ship can no longer safely sustain people onboard and abandonment or rescue is required.

In design terms, fire and flooding are treated separately because their damage propagation mechanisms differ: fire is controlled by containment, detection, suppression and redundancy; flooding is controlled by subdivision, buoyancy, stability, pumping and watertight integrity.

Casualty threshold

The casualty threshold is the maximum extent of damage, defined in the ship’s design basis, that the ship can sustain and still safely return to port. imo

Below threshold:

Casualty≤threshold⇒safe return to port under own propulsion \text{Casualty} \leq \text{threshold} \Rightarrow \text{safe return to port under own propulsion} Casualty≤threshold⇒safe return to port under own propulsion

Above threshold:

Casualty>threshold⇒ship must support orderly evacuation and abandonment \text{Casualty} > \text{threshold} \Rightarrow \text{ship must support orderly evacuation and abandonment} Casualty>threshold⇒ship must support orderly evacuation and abandonment

This is not a claim that the ship can survive every imaginable accident. It is a defined design standard that gives the master, crew and passengers a more reliable margin for foreseeable major casualties.

Essential systems for Safe Return

SOLAS II-2 Regulation 21 identifies systems expected to remain operational, in the unaffected part of the ship, following a fire casualty within the threshold. They include:

  • Propulsion.
  • Steering and steering control.
  • Navigation systems.
  • Fuel-oil filling, transfer and service systems.
  • Internal communications among bridge, engine spaces, safety centre, fire/damage-control teams, passengers and muster stations.
  • External communications.
  • Fire main and fixed extinguishing systems.
  • Fire and smoke detection.
  • Bilge and ballast systems.
  • Power-operated watertight and semi-watertight doors.
  • Flooding detection.
  • Systems supporting safe areas.
  • Other Administration-required systems vital to damage control. imorules

The design implication is redundancy and physical separation. For example, duplicate power cables must not be routed through the same fire zone if one fire can disable both; duplicate propulsion or steering capability must have sufficiently independent supporting systems.

Essential services in safe areas

A safe area is a protected onboard space where passengers and crew can be accommodated during return to port after a casualty within the threshold. It must provide:

  • Sanitation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Food.
  • Alternative medical-care space.
  • Shelter from weather.
  • Measures to avoid hypothermia or heat stress.
  • Lighting.
  • Ventilation. imorules

For a prolonged return-to-port situation, this is a practical humanitarian requirement, not a theoretical one. People cannot safely remain aboard for many hours without toilets, water, food, basic medical treatment, heat/cooling, light and air.

SAR in remote areas

In remote areas, immediate rescue may be unavailable because of distance, weather, lack of helicopters, few suitable vessels, weak communications or limited medical facilities ashore. A successful abandonment may still leave hundreds or thousands of persons in survival craft awaiting recovery.

IMO therefore developed:

  • Guidance on external support to assist incident containment.
  • Enhanced contingency-planning guidance for passenger ships in remote SAR areas.
  • Recovery-technique guidance.
  • Training guidance for SAR personnel in major incidents.
  • Cold-water survival guidance.
  • Voyage-planning guidance for passenger ships operating in remote areas. imo

The operational implication is straightforward: before entering remote waters, the company and master should identify likely rescue coordination centres, nearby vessels, diversion ports, helicopter range, medical resources, communication contingencies and expected recovery times.

Manila Statement and ferries

The Manila Statement on the Enhancement of the Safety of Ships Carrying Passengers on Non-International Voyages was adopted in Manila on 24 April 2015. It recognized continuing unacceptable loss of life in domestic-ferry accidents and emphasized that domestic ferries often fall outside international SOLAS application even though sea hazards do not distinguish between international and domestic services. wwwcdn.imo

Adequacy of the initiative

The initiative is valuable because it takes a fit-for-purpose, risk-based approach rather than attempting to impose every international SOLAS requirement unchanged on small, short-route domestic ferries.

It calls for national systems that address:

  • Vessel design, stability, freeboard, watertight integrity and structural strength.
  • Safe conversion or modification of second-hand vessels.
  • Reassessment when a ferry changes route, operating area or service limits.
  • Passenger counting and reliable records of all persons on board.
  • Proper voyage planning, weather information and navigational support.
  • Adequate crew competency, survey, inspection, certification and enforcement.
  • Fire detection, alarms, escape routes, lifesaving appliances, bilge arrangements and ro-ro deck drainage.
  • Investigation of casualties and implementation of lessons learned. wwwcdn.imo

Core regional problems

The Statement identifies recurring conditions that make coastal and inland ferry safety difficult, particularly in developing regions:

  • Fares may be too low to make services commercially viable without compromising maintenance, crew standards or vessel quality.
  • Old second-hand ships may be purchased for routes and weather conditions for which they were never designed.
  • Vessels may be converted without adequate engineering assessment or stability re-evaluation.
  • Ships may be moved from sheltered to exposed routes without reviewing service limits.
  • Commercial or social pressure may lead to passenger overloading.
  • Regulators may lack sufficiently trained surveyors, auditors, inspectors and examiners.
  • Weather forecasting, aids to navigation, radio communications and SAR infrastructure may be limited. wwwcdn.imo

Evaluation

The Manila approach is adequate in principle, because it recognizes that domestic operations need scalable, locally enforceable standards and promotes eventual safety equivalence with SOLAS and STCW rather than superficial paper compliance.

Its limitation is implementation. Guidance alone cannot prevent casualties unless States provide:

  • Effective legislation and independent enforcement.
  • Reliable passenger-counting controls.
  • Competent marine survey and inspection.
  • Route-specific design and weather limitations.
  • Training and certification systems for masters and crews.
  • Enforcement against overloading and unsafe conversions.
  • Investment in navigation aids, communications, emergency response and SAR.

A strong exam conclusion is:

The Manila Statement correctly treats domestic ferry safety as a shared responsibility of government, owners, operators, shipboard staff, regulators, ports, classification bodies, insurers and passengers. Its success depends not on the existence of guidelines, but on practical enforcement, competent people and vessels demonstrably suited to their route, weather exposure and passenger load. wwwcdn.imo

ROPAX and Tankers: Theory Specimen Questions and Answers

① Inherent Strength of Design: Oil Tanker vs. Dry Cargo Ship

A. Structural Strength Advantages of Tankers

1. Double Hull Design (MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 13)

  • Tankers:

    • Mandatory double hull (or double bottom + double sides) for oil tankers > 5,000 DWT (post-Exxon Valdez, 1989).
    • Reduces oil spill risk in grounding/collision.
    • Increases structural redundancy (two layers of hull plating).

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Typically single hull (except bulk carriers > 150m, which may have double sides for ballast tanks).

2. Longitudinal Strength

  • Tankers:

    • Continuous longitudinal bulkheads (centerline or side) reduce hogging/sagging stresses.
    • Cargo tanks act as structural members, contributing to longitudinal strength.
    • Higher section modulus (due to deep, box-like tanks).

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Open cargo holds (no longitudinal bulkheads) → lower section modulus.
    • More prone to hogging/sagging (especially in bulk carriers with large, empty holds).

3. Transverse Strength

  • Tankers:

    • Transverse bulkheads (every 2–4 tanks) resist racking stresses.
    • Wing tanks and double bottoms add transverse rigidity.

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Fewer transverse bulkheads (typically at 1/5 ship length intervals).
    • Higher racking stresses in open holds.

4. Fatigue Resistance

  • Tankers:

    • Smoother stress distribution due to liquid cargo (no point loads).
    • Corrosion protection (coatings, cathodic protection) mandatory in cargo tanks.

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Point loads from grain, ore, or containers → higher fatigue stress concentrations.
    • Corrosion in cargo holds (e.g., bulk carriers carrying salt, ore, or coal).

5. Stability Advantages

  • Tankers:

    • Lower KG (Vertical Center of Gravity): Liquid cargo (oil) fills tanks from the bottom up → lower VCG.
    • Free surface effect minimized (tanks are subdivided).
    • Higher GM (Metacentric Height) → stiffer ship (less rolling).

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Higher KG: Granular cargo (e.g., grain) can shift, raising VCG.
    • Free surface effect in partially filled holds.
    • Lower GM → tender ship (more rolling).

B. Freeboard Assignment Under ILLC (International Load Line Convention, 1966)

  • Tankers:

    • Assigned lesser freeboard than dry cargo ships of the same dimensions because:
      1. Lower KG → higher stability (less risk of capsizing).
      2. Double hull → better damage survivability (reduces risk of flooding).
      3. Subdivision (tanks act as watertight compartments) → better buoyancy after damage.
      4. ILLC Type B Freeboard: Tankers are classified as Type B (lower freeboard) due to higher stability and subdivision.

  • Dry Cargo Ships:

    • Assigned higher freeboard (Type A or B-60) due to:
      • Higher KG (less stable).
      • Open cargo holds → higher risk of flooding if damaged.
      • No subdivision in cargo holds → less damage survivability.

② Freeboard: Tanker vs. Bulk Carrier (Same Dimensions)

A. Why Tankers Have Lesser Freeboard

  1. Stability:

    • Tankers: Lower KG (liquid cargo) → higher GM → more stable.
    • Bulk Carriers: Higher KG (granular cargo) → lower GM → less stable.

  2. Subdivision & Damage Survivability:

    • Tankers:
      • Double hull → reduces flooding risk.
      • Cargo tanks are watertight → limits progressive flooding.
    • Bulk Carriers:
      • Single hull → higher flooding risk if damaged.
      • Open cargo holds → no subdivision → faster flooding.

  3. ILLC Classification:

    • Tankers: Type B (lower freeboard).
    • Bulk Carriers: Type A (higher freeboard).

B. Role of Pump Room Double Bottom & Cargo Pumps in Survivability

  1. Pump Room Double Bottom (MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 13G)

    • Mandatory for tankers > 5,000 DWT.
    • Prevents oil leakage in case of grounding or collision.
    • Acts as a secondary barrier → improves damage stability.

  2. Cargo Pumps

    • Located in pump rooms (separate from cargo tanks).
    • Submersible pumps (in each tank) reduce risk of oil spill in case of hull breach.
    • Remote-controlled valves → faster emergency shutdown.

  3. Survivability Benefits:

    • Reduces risk of oil pollution (environmental protection).
    • Enhances damage stability (fewer compartments flooded).
    • Compliance with SOLAS II-2 (Fire Safety) and MARPOL Annex I.

④ SOLAS-90 Standard for ROPAX Ships

A. SOLAS-90 Standard

  • Applies to: ROPAX ships (Roll-on/Roll-off Passenger Ships) built after 1 July 1990.
  • Key Requirements:
    1. Damage Stability:
      • Must survive flooding of any single compartment (including car deck).
      • Final GM ≥ 0.05 m after damage.
      • Maximum heel angle ≤ 15° in damaged condition.
    2. Subdivision:
      • Watertight bulkheads must extend to the freeboard deck.
      • Car decks must have watertight doors (automatically closed in case of fire/flooding).
    3. Fire Safety:
      • Fire-resistant divisions (A-60 class) around car decks and accommodation.
      • Fixed fire-extinguishing systems (e.g., water mist, CO₂).

B. SOLAS-90+ (50) Standard

  • Definition: An enhanced version of SOLAS-90, introduced after the Estonia disaster (1994).
  • Key Improvements:
    1. Increased Damage Stability:
      • Must survive flooding of any two adjacent compartments (not just one).
      • Final GM ≥ 0.10 m (higher than SOLAS-90).
    2. Stricter Subdivision:
      • Additional watertight bulkheads on car decks.
      • Higher freeboard (to reduce flooding risk).
    3. Enhanced Fire Safety:
      • Automatic sprinklers in car decks.
      • Improved ventilation control (fire dampers).

C. Stockholm Agreement (1996)

  • Context: After the Estonia disaster (1994), the IMO and EU agreed on stricter rules for ROPAX ships.
  • Key Decisions:
    1. Retrofitting Existing Ships:

    2. A and Amax:
      • A: Permissible damage length (maximum length of a single compartment that can flood without capsizing).
      • Amax: Maximum allowable damage length (based on ship’s dimensions and stability).
      • Compliance Requirement: A ≤ 0.5 × Amax (ship must survive flooding of half the maximum allowable damage length).
    3. Lines of Defense:
      • Primary: Watertight bulkheads.
      • Secondary: Fire-resistant divisions.
      • Tertiary: Improved evacuation systems (e.g., lifeboats on both sides).

## **⑥ Design Philosophy & Rulemaking for ROPAX Safety**

### **A. Multi-Pronged Approach to Safety**
The IMO and classification societies (e.g., DNV, LR, ABS) use a **layered approach** to improve ROPAX safety:

| **Layer** | **Objective** | **Examples (Rules & Regulations)** |
|-----------|---------------|------------------------------------|
| **1. Prevention** | Avoid accidents (fire, flooding, collision). | Fire-resistant materials (SOLAS II-2), Navigation equipment (SOLAS V), Training (STCW). |
| **2. Containment** | Limit damage if an accident occurs. | Watertight bulkheads (SOLAS II-1), Double hulls (MARPOL Annex I), Fire doors (SOLAS II-2). |
| **3. Mitigation** | Reduce consequences of accidents (e.g., flooding, fire). | Damage stability (SOLAS II-1, Reg. 8-4), Fixed fire extinguishing systems (SOLAS II-2, Reg. 10). |
| **4. Evacuation** | Ensure safe escape of passengers and crew. | Lifeboats on both sides (SOLAS III), Emergency lighting (SOLAS II-2, Reg. 13), Muster stations (SOLAS III). |
| **5. Survivability** | Improve chances of survival after an accident. | SOLAS-90+ (50) standards (enhanced damage stability), Stockholm Agreement (retrofitting). |

### **B. Rulemaking Process**
1. **Incident Analysis**: Investigate disasters (e.g., Estonia, Al Salaam Boccaccio 98) to identify weaknesses.
2. **Risk Assessment**: Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) to evaluate hazards and mitigation measures.
3. **Regulation Development**: IMO Sub-Committees (e.g., DE, FP, SDC) draft new rules. Class Societies provide technical guidelines.
4. **Implementation & Enforcement**: SOLAS amendments (e.g., SOLAS-90, SOLAS-90+ (50)). Port State Control (PSC) inspections to ensure compliance.

## **⑦ Fire Safety Design for Ro-Ro Ships (SOLAS Requirements)**

### **A. Definitions**
1. **Ro-Ro Space**:
   - A **cargo space** with **roll-on/roll-off access** (e.g., car decks, vehicle decks).
   - **Characteristics**: Large, open areas (no permanent subdivision). High fire risk (vehicles with fuel, batteries, etc.).
   - **SOLAS Definition**: "A space not normally subdivided in any way and extending to either the full width or the full length of the ship" (SOLAS II-2, Reg. 3.44).

2. **Special Category Space**:
   - A **cargo space** that is **not a Ro-Ro space** but has **similar fire risks** (e.g., spaces carrying dangerous goods, vehicles with fuel).
   - **SOLAS Definition**: "A space intended for the carriage of vehicles with fuel in their tanks for their own propulsion" (SOLAS II-2, Reg. 3.45).


---

### **B. Fire Safety Goals (SOLAS II-2, Part C)**

| **Goal** | **Ro-Ro Spaces** | **Special Category Spaces** |
|----------|------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Prevention** | No open flames in cargo areas. Hot work permits required. | Same as Ro-Ro spaces. No smoking in cargo areas. |
| **Detection** | Automatic fire detection (heat/smoke detectors). CCTV monitoring. | Same as Ro-Ro spaces. |
| **Containment** | A-60 class bulkheads around cargo spaces. Fire doors (A-60) on access points. | Same as Ro-Ro spaces. |
| **Extinction** | Fixed water-based fire-extinguishing system (e.g., water mist, sprinklers). Portable extinguishers (CO₂, dry chemical). | Fixed CO₂ or water mist system (for dangerous goods). Portable extinguishers. |
| **Structural Integrity** | Non-combustible materials (SOLAS II-2, Reg. 3). Thermal insulation to delay fire spread. | Same as Ro-Ro spaces. |
| **Ventilation Control** | Fire dampers in ventilation ducts. Automatic shutdown in case of fire. | Same as Ro-Ro spaces. |


---

### **C. SOLAS Requirements for Ro-Ro & Special Category Spaces**
1. **Fire Main System**: Hose reels and hydrants must cover **all Ro-Ro spaces**.
2. **Fixed Fire-Extinguishing Systems**:
   - **Water mist or sprinklers** (for Ro-Ro spaces).
   - **CO₂ or foam** (for special category spaces with flammable cargo).
3. **Fire Doors**:
   - **A-60 class** (fire-resistant for 60 minutes).
   - **Self-closing and remotely controlled**.
4. **Ventilation**:
   - **Fire dampers** in **all ventilation ducts** serving Ro-Ro spaces.
   - **Automatic closure** in case of fire.
5. **Structural Fire Protection**:
   - **Bulkheads and decks** around Ro-Ro spaces must be **A-60 class**.
   - **Insulation** to prevent **heat transfer** to adjacent spaces.

## **⑧ Corrosion in Tankers (or Bulk Carriers) & Regulatory Solutions**

### **A. Corrosion Problems in Tankers**

| **Area** | **Type of Corrosion** | **Causes** | **Impact** |
|----------|-----------------------|------------|------------|
| **1. Cargo Tanks** | General Corrosion (uniform thinning). | Sulfur in crude oil (forms H₂S, which reacts with steel). Water in cargo (electrolyte for corrosion). | Reduced plate thickness → structural failure. Leaks → oil pollution. |
| **2. Ballast Tanks** | Pitting Corrosion (localized deep pits). | Seawater (high chloride content). Poor coating maintenance. | Holes in tanks → flooding risk. Reduced structural strength. |
| **3. Double Bottom** | Crevice Corrosion (in gaps between plates). | Stagnant water in ballast tanks. Poor drainage. | Cracks in welds → leaks. Loss of watertight integrity. |
| **4. Deck & Superstructure** | Atmospheric Corrosion (rusting). | Salt spray (marine environment). Lack of paint maintenance. | Aesthetic damage. Weakened superstructure. |
| **5. Pipelines & Valves** | Erosion-Corrosion (flow-induced wear). | High-velocity oil/water flow. Abrasive particles (sand, scale). | Leaks in pipes → cargo loss/pollution. Valve failure. |


---

### **B. Regulatory Solutions to Corrosion**

| **Regulation** | **Requirement** | **Impact** |
|----------------|-----------------|------------|
| **1. MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 13G** | Double Hull for Tankers (>5,000 DWT). | Reduces oil spill risk in grounding/collision. Corrosion in one hull does not affect the other. |
| **2. SOLAS II-1, Reg. 3-11** | Corrosion Prevention in Ballast Tanks: Coatings (e.g., epoxy, zinc-rich). Cathodic Protection (sacrificial anodes or impressed current). | Extends tank life by 15–20 years. Reduces pitting corrosion. |
| **3. IACS UR Z10.4** | Enhanced Survey Requirements for Tankers: Close-up surveys every 5 years. Ultrasonic Thickness Measurements (UTM) for cargo/ballast tanks. | Early detection of corrosion. Prevents sudden structural failure. |
| **4. SOLAS II-2, Reg. 4.5.5** | Fire-Resistant Coatings in Cargo Tanks (for crude oil tankers). | Delays structural failure in case of fire. |
| **5. IMO PSPC (Performance Standard for Protective Coatings)** | Mandatory high-quality coatings for ballast tanks (resolution MSC.215(82)). | Reduces corrosion rate by 50–70%. |
| **6. Class Society Rules (e.g., ABS, DNV, LR)** | Corrosion Margins: Additional plate thickness (e.g., 2–3 mm extra in high-risk areas). | Compensates for expected corrosion over the ship’s life. |
