Ship Design, Shipbuilding Cost Models, and Trials

1. Cost Models in Ship Design and Shipbuilding

A. Overview of Cost Models

Cost models in shipbuilding are used to estimate, budget, and optimize expenses across the design, construction, and operational phases. These models help shipyards and owners predict costs, allocate resources, and ensure profitability. Common cost models include:

Cost Model Description Application
Parametric Cost Models Use historical data and statistical relationships to estimate costs based on ship parameters (e.g., DWT, LOA, speed). Early-stage conceptual design and feasibility studies.
Analogous Cost Models Estimate costs based on similar past projects (e.g., a new bulk carrier vs. a previously built one). Preliminary design and budgeting.
Bottom-Up Cost Models Break down the ship into components (hull, machinery, outfitting) and sum their individual costs. Detailed design and contract bidding.
Cost Estimating Relationships (CER) Mathematical equations linking ship characteristics (e.g., displacement, power) to cost. Quick cost estimates during feasibility and conceptual design.
Activity-Based Costing (ABC) Allocates costs based on activities (e.g., welding, painting, assembly). Production planning and process optimization.
Learning Curve Models Account for efficiency gains as production progresses (e.g., reduced labor hours per unit). Serial production (e.g., building multiple ships of the same design).

2. Cost Estimating Relationship (CER)

A. Definition

A Cost Estimating Relationship (CER) is a mathematical or statistical model that relates ship characteristics (e.g., displacement, length, power) to cost. CERs are derived from historical data and regression analysis.

B. Types of CERs

Type Description Example
Simple Linear CER Cost = a + b × (Ship Parameter). Cost = 5,000,000 + 20,000 × (DWT)
Power Law CER Cost = a × (Ship Parameter)^b. Cost = 10,000 × (LOA)^1.7
Multiple Regression CER Cost = a + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + … + bₙXₙ (where X₁, X₂, etc., are ship parameters like DWT, speed, etc.). Cost = 2,000,000 + 15,000 × (DWT) + 50,000 × (Speed)

C. Advantages of CERs

  • Quick estimates: Useful for early-stage design when detailed data is unavailable.
  • Scalability: Can be applied to different ship sizes within a class (e.g., bulk carriers, tankers).
  • Data-driven: Based on historical trends, reducing subjective bias.

D. Limitations of CERs

  • Accuracy depends on data quality: Poor historical data leads to unreliable estimates.
  • Assumes linearity: May not capture non-linear cost drivers (e.g., complex machinery).
  • Less accurate for innovative designs: Works best for conventional ships with existing data.

E. Example CER for Shipbuilding

For a bulk carrier, a CER might look like:

Cost (USD) = 12,000,000 + 18,000 × (DWT) + 30,000 × (Engine Power in kW)

Where:

  • DWT = Deadweight Tonnage
  • Engine Power = Main engine power in kW

3. Hull Block Construction Method (HBCM)

A. Definition

The Hull Block Construction Method (HBCM) is a modular shipbuilding approach where the hull is constructed in pre-fabricated blocks (sections) that are later assembled in the dry dock or on the slipway. This method is widely used in modern shipyards (e.g., Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries).

B. Cost Savings in HBCM

Cost-Saving Factor Explanation
Reduced Labor in Dry Dock Blocks are pre-fabricated in workshops, reducing on-site labor and construction time.
Parallel Processing Different blocks can be built simultaneously, shortening the total build time.
Improved Quality Control Workshop conditions allow for better precision and fewer rework costs.
Economies of Scale Bulk material procurement and standardized processes reduce costs.
Reduced Dry Dock Time Blocks are assembled quickly in the dry dock, minimizing dock rental costs.
Lower Skilled Labor Needs Pre-fabrication reduces the need for highly skilled labor on-site.

C. HBCM Process

  1. Block Design: Hull is divided into 3D-modeled blocks (e.g., bow, midship, stern).
  2. Pre-Fabrication: Blocks are cut, welded, and outfitted in workshops.
  3. Transport: Blocks are moved to the dry dock using cranes or transporters.
  4. Assembly: Blocks are welded together to form the hull.
  5. Outfitting: Piping, electrical, and machinery are installed.

4. Advantages of Pre-Fabrication

A. Cost and Time Savings

Advantage Explanation
Reduced Construction Time Parallel processing of blocks shortens the total build schedule.
Lower Labor Costs Workshop-based fabrication reduces on-site labor and overhead costs.
Better Working Conditions Workers operate in controlled environments (e.g., covered workshops), improving productivity and safety.
Higher Precision CNC cutting and automated welding improve dimensional accuracy, reducing rework.
Material Efficiency Optimized nesting (cutting patterns) reduces steel wastage.
Easier Quality Control Inspection and testing are easier in a workshop setting.
Reduced Weather Delays Indoor fabrication minimizes weather-related disruptions.

B. Examples of Pre-Fabrication

  • Hull Blocks: Pre-welded sections of the hull.
  • Pipe Spools: Pre-fabricated piping systems.
  • Electrical Panels: Pre-assembled and tested electrical distribution boards.
  • Accommodation Modules: Pre-built living quarters (e.g., cabins, galleys).

5. Estimating Finished Steel Weight of a Ship

A. Methods for Estimating Steel Weight

Method Description Accuracy Stage of Design
Parametric Estimation Uses CERs or statistical formulas based on ship dimensions (e.g., L × B × D). Low Conceptual Design
Lightweight Analysis Breaks down the ship into structural components (hull, decks, bulkheads) and sums their weights. Medium Preliminary Design
3D CAD Modeling Uses detailed 3D models (e.g., NAPA, CADMATIC) to calculate exact steel weights. High Contract Design
Class Society Rules Uses classification society formulas (e.g., Lloyd’s Register, ABS, DNV) for minimum scantlings. Medium All Stages

B. Parametric Formula for Steel Weight

A simple parametric formula for estimating steel weight (for a bulk carrier):

Steel Weight (tons) = C × (L × B × D)^(2/3)

Where:

  • L = Length Overall (m)
  • B = Breadth (m)
  • D = Depth (m)
  • C = Constant (varies by ship type, e.g., 0.015–0.025 for bulk carriers)

C. Lightweight Analysis

  1. Hull Girder Weight:
    • Bottom, side, deck plating + longitudinals, transverses, webs, and stiffeners.
  2. Superstructure Weight:
    • Accommodation, bridge, funnel (if applicable).
  3. Outfitting Weight:
    • Piping, electrical systems, machinery supports (if included in steel weight).

6. Basic Ship Design vs. New Ship Design

A. Basic Ship Design (Shipyard’s Standard Design)

  • Definition: A proven, standardized design that the shipyard has built before (e.g., a Newcastlemax bulk carrier or a Suezmax tanker).
  • Characteristics:
    • Pre-existing drawings, calculations, and specifications.
    • Optimized for construction efficiency (e.g., pre-fabricated blocks, standardized materials).
    • Lower design costs (no R&D required).
    • Faster delivery (familiar to the shipyard).

B. New Ship Design (Custom Design)

  • Definition: A bespoke design tailored to the owner’s specific requirements (e.g., a specialized LNG carrier or a polar icebreaker).
  • Characteristics:
    • Unique hull form, machinery, and outfitting.
    • Higher design costs (R&D, model testing, class approval).
    • Longer delivery time (new tooling, training, and processes).
    • Higher risk (unproven performance, potential cost overruns).

C. Narrowing the Differences

To bridge the gap between a basic design and a new design, the following steps are taken:

Step Description
Feasibility Study Assess technical and economic viability of the new design.
Parametric Comparisons Compare key dimensions (LOA, DWT, speed) with existing designs.
Model Testing Conduct towing tank tests or CFD analysis to validate performance.
Class Society Approval Obtain preliminary approval from classification societies (e.g., ABS, DNV, LR).
Modular Adaptations Use pre-existing modules (e.g., engine room, accommodation) from basic designs.
Cost-Benefit Analysis Evaluate trade-offs between customization and cost.
Iterative Design Refinement Gradually refine the design through multiple iterations (see Design Spiral below).

7. Slog-Slog Method

A. Definition

The “Slog-Slog” method (also called the “Log-Log” method) is a graphical cost estimation technique used in shipbuilding to compare costs across different ship sizes or designs. It involves plotting cost vs. ship parameter (e.g., DWT, LOA) on a logarithmic scale for both axes.

B. When is it Used?

  • Early-stage cost estimation (when detailed data is unavailable).
  • Comparing costs of different ship sizes (e.g., scaling a 50,000 DWT bulk carrier to 80,000 DWT).
  • Benchmarking against industry standards.

C. How It Works

  1. Plot historical data (cost vs. ship parameter) on a log-log graph.
  2. Draw a best-fit line (represents the cost trend).
  3. Use the line to estimate costs for new ship sizes.

D. Example

If the cost of a 50,000 DWT bulk carrier is $30M, and the cost of a 100,000 DWT bulk carrier is $50M, the Slog-Slog method can estimate the cost of a 75,000 DWT bulk carrier by interpolating on the log-log plot.

8. Estimating Labour and Material Costs in Shipbuilding

A. Labour Cost Estimation

Factor Method
Man-Hours per Task Estimate labor hours for each task (e.g., welding, painting, assembly) based on historical data.
Wage Rates Multiply man-hours by hourly wage rates (varies by country and skill level).
Productivity Factors Adjust for worker efficiency (e.g., learning curve, fatigue, experience).
Overhead Costs Include supervision, training, and administrative costs.

Formula for Labour Cost 

Labour Cost = Σ (Man-Hours × Hourly Rate × Productivity Factor)

B. Material Cost Estimation

Factor Method
Steel Weight Estimated using CERs or 3D modeling (see Section 5).
Unit Cost of Steel Multiply steel weight by cost per ton (varies by market prices).
Other Materials Include paint, piping, electrical components, machinery, and outfitting.
Wastage Factor Account for cutting and fabrication waste (typically 5–15% of total material).

Formula for Material Cost 

Material Cost = (Steel Weight × Cost per Ton) + (Other Materials Cost) × (1 + Wastage Factor)

C. Productivity Factors

Productivity factors adjust labour and material cost estimates to account for real-world conditions. Common factors include:

Factor Impact on Cost Example
Learning Curve Reduces labour hours as workers gain experience (e.g., 90% learning curve). After building 10 ships, labour hours per ship may drop by 10–20%.
Work Environment Harsh conditions (e.g., extreme weather, confined spaces) increase labour time. Welding in a cold, open dry dock may require 20% more time than in a workshop.
Skill Level Higher-skilled workers are more efficient but cost more per hour. A certified welder may cost $50/hr vs. $30/hr for an apprentice.
Tooling and Equipment Advanced tools (e.g., automated welding, CNC cutting) reduce labour time. Robotic welding can reduce labour costs by 30–40%.
Fatigue Long shifts or overtime can reduce productivity by 10–20%. Workers on 12-hour shifts may be 15% less productive than on 8-hour shifts.
Quality Control Rework due to defects increases labour and material costs. 10% rework rate can add 5–10% to total costs.

9. Ship Trials

A. Overview of Ship Trials

Ship trials are conducted to verify the performance, safety, and compliance of a newly built or refitted ship. They are typically divided into:

  1. Harbour Acceptance Trials (HAT): Basic checks in port (e.g., engine startup, navigation equipment).
  2. Sea Acceptance Trials (SAT): Performance tests at sea (e.g., speed, maneuvering, fuel consumption).
  3. Final Acceptance Trials: Comprehensive tests before delivery to the owner.

B. Measured Mile Trial

A. Purpose

  • Measure the ship’s speed and power performance under controlled conditions.
  • Verify contractual speed and fuel consumption guarantees.

B. Procedure

  1. Selection of Measured Mile: A calibrated, straight track (typically 1–2 nautical miles long) with known current and tide conditions.
  2. Test Conditions:
    • Calm weather (Beaufort Scale ≤ 3, wave height ≤ 1.25 m).
    • Stable loading (ballast or cargo as per contract).
    • Engine at MCR (Maximum Continuous Rating) or specified power.
  3. Measurements:
    • Speed over ground (SOG) (using GPS or Doppler log).
    • Speed through water (STW) (using a paddle wheel log or electromagnetic log).
    • Engine parameters (RPM, fuel consumption, exhaust temperature).
    • Propeller shaft power (using a torsion meter).

C. Data Analysis

  • Speed-Power Curve: Plots ship speed vs. engine power to verify contractual performance.
  • Fuel Consumption Analysis: Compares actual fuel consumption vs. guaranteed values at different speeds.
  • Hull Efficiency: Assesses hull cleanliness and fouling impact on performance.

C. Fuel Consumption Trial

A. Inputs to be Measured and Recorded

Category Inputs
Ship Parameters Displacement, draft, trim, stability (GM), wind and current conditions.
Engine Parameters Engine RPM, fuel flow rate, fuel density, exhaust gas temperature, turbocharger pressure.
Propulsion Parameters Propeller pitch, shaft RPM, torque, thrust.
Environmental Conditions Air temperature, humidity, sea temperature, wave height, wind speed/direction.
Navigation Data GPS position, speed over ground (SOG), speed through water (STW), course.

B. Outputs to be Measured and Recorded

Category Outputs
Performance Metrics Maximum speed at MCR, fuel consumption at various speeds, specific fuel consumption (SFC).
Engine Efficiency Brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), thermal efficiency.
Propulsion Efficiency Propulsive efficiency, hull efficiency, wake fraction.
Emissions Data CO₂, NOx, SOx emissions (for compliance with IMO 2020, EEXI, CII).
Vibration and Noise Vibration levels (in engine room, accommodation), noise levels (dB).

D. Ship Maneuvering Trials

A. Turning Circle Trial

  • Purpose: Measure the ship’s turning ability and tactical diameter.
  • Procedure:
    1. Ship approaches the turning point at steady speed (e.g., 80% of service speed).
    2. Hard starboard/port rudder (typically 35°) is applied.
    3. Turning circle is recorded using GPS or radar tracking.
  • Key Metrics:
    • Tactical Diameter: Distance between the initial and final course lines (should be ≤ 5 × LOA for most ships).
    • Advance: Distance traveled along the original course before the ship turns 90°.
    • Transfer: Distance traveled perpendicular to the original course when the ship turns 90°.
    • Time to Turn 90°: Should be ≤ 2–3 minutes for most commercial ships.

B. Crash Stop Trial

  • Purpose: Measure the ship’s stopping ability in an emergency.
  • Procedure:
    1. Ship is brought to full ahead speed (e.g., 80–100% MCR).
    2. Full astern power is applied, and engine is reversed (if applicable).
    3. Stopping distance and time are recorded.
  • Key Metrics:
    • Stopping Distance: Distance traveled from full ahead to full stop (should be ≤ 15 × LOA for most ships).
    • Stopping Time: Time taken to come to a complete stop (typically 10–20 minutes for large ships).
    • Head Reach: Distance traveled ahead of the initial position before stopping.

C. Fuel Consumption at MCR

  • Purpose: Verify fuel efficiency at Maximum Continuous Rating (MCR).
  • Procedure:
    1. Ship is brought to MCR power (100% engine load).
    2. Fuel consumption is measured over a steady-state period (e.g., 1–2 hours).
    3. Exhaust emissions are analyzed for compliance.
  • Key Metrics:
    • Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC): kg of fuel per kWh (should match contractual guarantees).
    • Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (BSFC): g/kWh (typically 170–210 g/kWh for modern diesel engines).
    • Emissions: CO₂, NOx, SOx (must comply with IMO Tier III, EEXI, CII).

Q1. VLCC vapour-space corrosion

The vapour space is the volume in a cargo tank above the liquid cargo level. In a VLCC carrying crude oil, it is commonly one of the most aggressive corrosion environments in the ship.

          Cargo-tank deck plating
     ─────────────────────────────────
       Vapour space: gases + moisture
       ↑ corrosive condensate zone
     ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~  Cargo oil surface
       Liquid crude-oil cargo

Reasons for accelerated corrosion

  1. Acidic gases occur in the inert-gas atmosphere

    Cargo tanks are commonly inerted to reduce explosion risk. However, inert gas and crude-oil vapours may contain oxygen, carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide. In the presence of condensed moisture, these gases form corrosive aqueous films and acidic products on deck plating, underdeck longitudinals and upper side structure. Field examinations of VLCC cargo tanks have found notable quantities of O2O_2O2​, CO2CO_2CO2​, SO2SO_2SO2​ and H2SH_2SH2​S, including high H2SH_2SH2​S concentrations in vapour spaces. classnk.or

    A simplified corrosion sequence is:

    SO2+H2O→acidic sulphur compounds SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow \text{acidic sulphur compounds} SO2​+H2​O→acidic sulphur compoundsCO2+H2O→H2CO3 CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3 CO2​+H2​O→H2​CO3​

    These wet, acidic films accelerate oxidation of steel:

    Fe→Fe2++2e− Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2e^- Fe→Fe2++2e−

  2. Condensation and wet–dry cycling

    The upper tank structure is alternately heated by cargo and cooled by night air, seawater or ballast water in adjacent spaces. Water vapour condenses on the relatively cool steel, producing an electrolyte film. Repeated wetting and drying concentrates salts and acidic contaminants, often making corrosion more severe than continuous immersion corrosion.

  3. High cargo temperature

    Some crude oils are loaded warm, and heated cargoes create significant temperature gradients. The vapour space, deck and upper shell are subjected to thermal cycling. Higher temperature generally increases electrochemical reaction rates and promotes condensation on adjacent cooler surfaces.

  4. Oxygen is not always absent

    Inerting reduces oxygen concentration but does not make every local environment chemically inert. Tank opening, loading/discharging, tank washing, imperfect inert gas quality, leaks and local air ingress can introduce oxygen. Corrosion is particularly severe where water, oxygen and corrosive gases coexist.

  5. Salt contamination

    Seawater contamination, salt deposits, ballast-tank leakage, washing water, poor tank cleaning and humid marine atmosphere can create chloride-rich electrolyte films. Chlorides promote local attack and interfere with coating durability.

  6. Coating damage and poor access

    The underside of deck plating, deck longitudinals, bracket toes, welds and upper-frame connections are difficult to blast, coat, inspect and repair. Damage to protective coating exposes bare steel, and local corrosion cells form rapidly at edges, welds and damaged areas.

  Underdeck longitudinals  ← major target
  Brackets and weld toes   ← local attack
  Upper transverse webs    ← coating damage
  Upper wing-tank boundary ← thermal gradient
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~  oil surface

  • Underside of deck plating.
  • Deck longitudinals and their web/flange edges.
  • Brackets, scallops, weld toes and cut-outs.
  • Upper parts of transverse bulkheads and longitudinal bulkheads.
  • Upper side-shell and upper wing-tank interfaces.

Q2. Pitting corrosion and pollution risk

Definition

Pitting corrosion is highly localized corrosion that produces small, deep cavities or pits in steel. It differs from general corrosion, which thins a broad area more uniformly.

General wastage                    Pitting corrosion

Steel surface                      Steel surface
──────────────                     ────┬──────┬────
  ↓ uniform thinning                   │  ↓   │
──────────────                     ────┴─┐ ┌─┴────
                                            └── deep pit

A plate may appear generally acceptable, yet a few pits can penetrate a large fraction of its original thickness.

Why pitting occurs in cargo tanks

Pitting is caused by local electrochemical cells created where conditions differ over small areas of steel.

Typical causes are:

  • Breakdown, blistering, cracking or mechanical damage to coating.
  • Water droplets, tank-wash water or salt deposits trapped in local depressions.
  • Chloride contamination from seawater.
  • Oxygen concentration differences between the centre and edges of a wet deposit.
  • Acidic condensate in the vapour space.
  • Sludge, scale, cargo residues or microbial activity that create differential aeration cells.
  • Weld defects, rough surfaces, edges, attachment points and coating holidays.
  • Galvanic differences between bare steel, coated steel, weld metal and deposits.

Pollution consequences

Pitting is particularly serious in:

  • Bottom plating of cargo tanks.
  • Inner-bottom plating in double-hull tankers.
  • Bulkheads separating cargo and ballast tanks.
  • Cargo tank boundaries adjacent to void spaces.
  • Shell plating in single-hull tankers.
Cargo oil tank                    Sea / ballast space

  Oil cargo
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
        steel plate
───────────────┐
      pitting  │  deepens
        ↓      │
───────────┐   │
           └───┘  → perforation → oil leakage

The pollution potential rises because pitting can produce a through-thickness perforation without a dramatic visible structural failure. Oil can leak:

  • Into a ballast tank or void space, becoming difficult to detect immediately.
  • Into the double bottom, contaminating ballast or bilge systems.
  • Directly to sea in a single-hull or externally damaged boundary.
  • Into spaces where vapour accumulation also creates fire and explosion hazards.

A small pit can also act as a crack initiator. If it occurs in a highly stressed plate, cyclic loading may turn local wastage into a fatigue crack and then into a larger rupture.

Q3. Why deck and inner-bottom scantlings reduced

This question usually refers to design trends in earlier generations of tankers, especially where designers took advantage of improved structural arrangements and higher-strength steels. It should not be understood to mean that present rules permit unsafe steel reduction: current Common Structural Rules prescribe net scantlings, corrosion additions and minimum thicknesses. For example, modern rules impose specific inner-bottom requirements and set gross minimum thickness values for structural members in liquid tanks and double bottoms. iacs.s3.af-south-1.amazonaws

Main reasons

Reason Effect on scantling selection
Use of higher-tensile steel Higher yield strength permits a smaller required plate thickness for the same calculated strength, subject to buckling, fatigue and minimum-thickness requirements

The drawback of reduced initial scantlings is a lower margin for:

Q4. Casualties and high-risk transition zones

Why ballast-tank boundaries are vulnerable

Ballast tanks are a severe corrosion environment because they contain seawater, oxygen, chlorides, temperature variation and frequent wet–dry cycles. The most severe areas are often those adjacent to cargo tanks.

Warm oil cargo tank       Common bulkhead        Cold seawater ballast tank

   Heated cargo        │ steel boundary │          seawater + oxygen
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~│────────────────│~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
                       │                │
    Thermal cycling →  │ condensation → │ coating breakdown/corrosion

A bulkhead or plating panel can suffer corrosion from both sides:

  • Cargo-tank side: acidic vapour condensate, cargo residues and temperature effects.
  • Ballast-tank side: seawater corrosion, oxygen, chlorides, coating breakdown and microbial effects.

This double-sided deterioration reduces section modulus more rapidly than corrosion on one face alone.

Why transition zones are critical

A transition zone is where structural geometry, stiffness, material thickness, loading type or environment changes abruptly. Such zones concentrate stress and are preferred sites for fatigue initiation.

Examples include:

  • Boundary between cargo tank and ballast tank.
  • Connection of longitudinal bulkhead to transverse bulkhead.
  • Tank-top to hopper plating transition.
  • Deck longitudinal termination.
  • Bracket toes and end connections.
  • Cut-outs, lightening holes and scallops.
  • Change from high-tensile to mild steel.
  • Change in plate thickness.
  • End of a longitudinal girder.
  • Pump-room boundaries.
  • Sloping bulkheads and knuckles.
Longitudinal stiffener termination

───────────────┐
               │  abrupt stiffness change
               └───────
                  ↑
            fatigue/crack-prone zone

Tanker casualties

Erika, 1999. The single-hull tanker broke apart in heavy weather off France, causing major oil pollution. The case is widely associated with structural deterioration, corrosion and the vulnerability of an ageing single-hull tanker. It helped intensify regulatory pressure for accelerated phase-out of single-hull oil tankers.

Prestige, 2002. The Prestige suffered a hull breach and subsequently broke up off Spain, causing a major spill. The Bahamas investigation identified a probable initial breach associated with a large wave exposing weakness in No. 3 starboard wing tank; it specifically noted that corrosion-related weakening of tanker ballast-tank structure is a well-documented problem and that the reported breaches were consistent with such weakness. bahamasmaritime

Nakhodka, 1997. The tanker broke in severe weather off Japan, leading to heavy fuel-oil pollution. The incident is often used to illustrate the vulnerability of older single-hull tanker structures to combined wave loading, ageing and deterioration.

Aegean Sea, 1992. Grounding and hull damage off La Coruña led to oil release and fire; while this is principally a grounding case, it demonstrates why loss of shell integrity in a loaded oil tanker has major environmental consequences.

Examination comment

A strong conclusion is:

Corrosion does not act in isolation. It reduces thickness, which increases stress; increased stress promotes fatigue; fatigue cracks concentrate at details and transition zones; and a large wave, grounding event or sloshing load may then trigger a sudden structural failure. The danger is greatest where a common boundary plate is exposed to corrosive environments on both sides and where geometry creates stress concentration.

Q5. Ballast-tank corrosion prevention

SOLAS protective-coating requirements

SOLAS Chapter II-1 includes mandatory protective-coating requirements through the Performance Standard for Protective Coatings (PSPC).

  • SOLAS II-1/3-2 applies the PSPC to dedicated seawater ballast tanks in all ship types and to double-side skin spaces of bulk carriers.
  • SOLAS II-1/3-11 applies PSPC requirements to cargo oil tanks of crude-oil tankers.
  • The prescribed coating systems are intended to achieve a target useful coating life of 15 years. ww2.eagle

For tanker ballast tanks, the relevant concept is PSPC for dedicated seawater ballast tanks, commonly linked to IMO Resolution MSC.215(82) and subsequent amendments. iims-media-library.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws

What a compliant prevention strategy requires 

Good design
     +
Correct surface preparation
     +
Specified coating system
     +
Controlled application
     +

1. Compliance with coating performance standards

Key elements include:

  • Steel surface preparation to the specified cleanliness grade.
  • Removal of weld spatter, sharp edges and surface imperfections.
  • Correct stripe coating at edges, welds, brackets, scallops and difficult details.
  • Correct dry-film thickness.
  • Controlled temperature, dew point, relative humidity and steel-surface condition during application.
  • Inspection and documentation during construction.
  • Coating technical file and maintenance records.
  • Use of a qualified coating inspector and appropriate owner/class/shipyard quality control.

The coating is a system, not merely a layer of paint. Poor edge preparation, inadequate stripe coating or application outside environmental limits can cause early failure even if the nominal dry-film thickness appears satisfactory.

2. Why the initial coating is crucial

The first coating application is the most important because it is applied in a controlled newbuilding environment before the tank enters service.

A high-quality initial coating:

  • Prevents corrosion before it begins.
  • Reduces under-film corrosion.
  • Keeps the tank surface smooth and easier to inspect.
  • Reduces later steel renewal and repair cost.
  • Limits the formation of pits that may become crack initiators.
  • Makes subsequent maintenance more practical.

Poor initial coating can lead to:

Minor holiday / edge defect
        ↓
Under-film corrosion
        ↓
Blistering and coating disbondment
        ↓
Large exposed area
        ↓
General wastage + pitting
        ↓
Steel renewal / structural risk

3. Why in-service recoating is difficult

Repairing coating in a ballast tank is much more difficult than applying the original coating because:

  • Access is restricted and ventilation is limited.
  • The space is enclosed, creating health and gas-safety hazards.
  • Surfaces are contaminated with salt, rust, oil, scale and old coating residues.
  • Complete abrasive blasting is difficult around complex stiffeners, brackets and pipework.
  • Humidity, temperature and dew point may not remain within ideal application limits.
  • Tank schedules compete with cargo operations, dry-docking and commercial pressure.
  • Temporary ventilation, lighting, staging and safety arrangements are costly.
  • Spot repair may leave adjacent marginal coating that subsequently fails.

Hence the practical rule is:

It is far cheaper and safer to achieve high-quality surface preparation and coating at newbuilding than to recover a severely corroded ballast tank after years of service.

Survey consequences of poor coating

Where hard protective coating was not applied at construction, is soft or semi-hard, is in poor condition and not repaired, or substantial corrosion is found, ballast tanks are subject to annual examination requirements in the enhanced survey regime. classnk.or

Q6. Fatigue cracks: causes and inspection targets

Why fatigue cracks occur

Fatigue cracking occurs when a structural detail experiences repeated cyclic stress. The stress range may be below the steel’s static yield strength, but repeated thousands or millions of times it can initiate and propagate a crack.

Repeated wave loading

Hogging → sagging → hogging → sagging → hogging
   ↑          ↓
Repeated stress range at structural detail
                     ↓
               fatigue crack

The principal sources of cyclic loading are:

  • Hull-girder hogging and sagging in waves.
  • Torsional loading, especially near large deck openings or discontinuities.
  • Sloshing loads in partly filled tanks.
  • Pressure cycling in ballast tanks.
  • Vibration from main engines, shafting, propellers and pumps.
  • Thermal expansion and contraction.
  • Repeated local bending of stiffeners and brackets.
  • Cargo loading/discharging cycles.
  • Berthing, grounding and impact loads.

Where to look

Routine inspection should focus on places with high stress concentration, reduced stiffness or known coating damage:

  • Weld toes and weld ends.
  • Bracket toes and bracket terminations.
  • Stiffener end connections.
  • Connections between longitudinals and transverse webs.
  • Cut-outs, manholes, lightening holes and scallops.
  • Corners of openings.
  • Change in plate thickness.
  • Change in framing system.
  • Intersections of bulkheads, girders and stringers.
  • Deck longitudinals near hatch ends and deckhouse ends.
  • Tank-top and inner-bottom connections.
  • Transverse web frame connections in wing ballast tanks.
  • Pump-room bulkheads and lower stool areas.
  • Bilge wells, drain holes and areas below sounding pipes.
  • Areas around cargo heating systems and pipe supports.

Areas needing stringent inspection

More stringent close-up survey and thickness gauging should target:

  • Cargo-tank deck structure in the vapour space.
  • Upper parts of transverse bulkheads.
  • Ballast-tank transverse webs and web-frame connections.
  • Lower parts of wing tanks and hopper-like regions where water and sediment collect.
  • Inner-bottom plating adjacent to cargo-tank/ballast-tank boundaries.
  • Shell plating and internal structure in the midship 0.4L0.4L0.4L region, where hull-girder bending is highest.
  • Known substantial-corrosion areas and adjacent structure.
  • Previously repaired cracks, doublers, insert plates and weld repairs.
  • Locations with poor, rusted, blistered or detached coating.

Q7. Limitations of surveys and thickness measurements

Thickness measurement—normally ultrasonic—is essential, but it cannot by itself establish whether a tanker is structurally safe.

Limitation 1: Measurements are discrete samples

Ultrasonic readings are taken at selected points, whereas corrosion may be highly localized.

A few readings may show acceptable average thickness while a small pit or groove between points is near perforation.

Limitation 2: General wastage versus local damage

UT is good for measuring remaining thickness at the measurement point, but interpretation is required to distinguish:

  • Uniform general corrosion.
  • Local pitting.
  • Grooving along welds.
  • Edge corrosion.
  • Crack-like defects.
  • Lamination or internal defects.
  • Under-deposit corrosion.

A plate may satisfy average-thickness criteria while still having unacceptable local pitting or severe grooving.

Limitation 3: Surface condition affects reliability

Rust scale, coating, roughness, marine deposits and poor probe contact can affect reading quality. Calibration, competent operators and surveyor oversight are therefore necessary. IACS guidance states that ultrasonic equipment accuracy must be proven and that measurements should be representative of the nature and extent of wastage; qualified companies perform the work and surveyors verify it. iacs.s3.af-south-1.amazonaws

Limitation 4: Access restrictions

Many critical locations are difficult to inspect:

  • High underdeck areas.
  • Behind piping and cables.
  • Inside narrow wing tanks.
  • Bracket toes and small scallops.
  • Areas behind stiffeners.
  • Tank corners and bilges.
  • Structures obscured by scale or coating.
  • Deep tanks requiring staging, rafting or remote inspection tools.

If access is poor, a survey can become biased toward accessible, less critical surfaces.

Limitation 5: Coating can conceal corrosion

A coating may look intact while corrosion progresses beneath it. Conversely, a visibly poor coating does not always indicate the exact remaining steel thickness. Coating condition is a warning indicator, not a substitute for thickness gauging.

Limitation 6: UT does not reliably detect cracks

Normal thickness gauging is not a crack-detection technique. Fatigue cracks need close visual inspection and, when required:

  • Magnetic particle inspection.
  • Dye penetrant testing.
  • Ultrasonic flaw detection.
  • Eddy-current testing.
  • Appropriate non-destructive testing of weld details.

Limitation 7: Structure is a system, not a set of plates

The residual strength of a tanker depends on more than individual plate thickness:

[ \text{Residual structural capacity}

f(\text{plate thickness},\text{stiffeners},\text{buckling},\text{fatigue},\text{connections},\text{load path},\text{global bending}) ]

A structure may fail by local buckling, stiffener tripping, bracket failure, crack propagation or loss of continuity before a simple plate-thickness limit is reached.

Limitation 8: Corrosion can progress between surveys

Survey intervals create a time gap. In severe ballast-tank or cargo-vapour-space environments, coating failure and corrosion may develop quickly between scheduled examinations, especially if the vessel experiences unusual heating, poor ballast-water quality, extended idle periods or damage.

Limitation 9: Human and commercial factors

Survey effectiveness may be reduced by:

  • Incomplete tank cleaning.
  • Inadequate lighting or staging.
  • Time pressure in dry dock.
  • Incomplete access.
  • Inadequate documentation of prior repairs.
  • Poor communication between owner, class, yard and thickness-measurement company.
  • Over-reliance on minimum numerical compliance rather than engineering judgement.
